Journal Entry: 3 meanings. 2 seconds. 1 button. One button press is enough for this sound to explode and fill the air with energy. Two seconds of bursting sound before the laughs. Three different meanings when it is heard. Could it be sarcastic? Could it be exaggerative? Could it be an embarrassment? The bustling explosion of only a single word from a speaker can ignite the crowd, creating a funny moment or a miss. A simple sound recognized by any 19 year old and yet it makes your brain react no matter how hard you try. Always reminding everyone who hears it, this sound is gonna make you laugh, enjoy it.

There’s ringing, and then there’s her breath. Ringing, breath. Ringing, ringing. Breath. Small sleeping puffs, out the nose. High ringing, ringing inside the ears. Ringing against the forehead. Breath. Loud ringing. So quiet that it screams at you. Breath. High and faint, fanning away, hissing like dried fingers rubbing against each other next to the external ear. Breath. Ringing. Breath that eases past the throat. Low breath, sighing breath. Dreaming breath. The quiet eliminates the material world.

Think Jurassic Park, four-wheel drive, off-roading in a pristine jungle with the mileage per hour necessitated to escape a T. rex’s claws and jaws; a sonic landscape far from the reality of the traversal of a tame—albeit potholed—black pavement roundabout. A synthesized round, high-end, and fast pulse accompanies the brute mechanical sound; the same sound of the faulty A/C in my mom’s totaled 2001 Nissan Altima.

Outside trees rustle. The shrill shriek of the little dog’s voice. It runs from the top of the house to the bottom, muffled vaguely but becoming louder and louder as she approaches. The rhythmic pattern of the buttons make little beeps, uniform in sound and loudness. I know by the sound if I did it right. The dog keeps barking, excitedly. Gravel under my feet makes crunching noises as I stand, and birds sing in the trees above. Urgency in her voice, endless excitement ahead. My favorite time of day.

The sounds of home. The moment the beat drops, it’s as if the air itself shifts—charged with rhythm, memory, and joy. The speakers explode with the electrifying pulse of Afrobeats, a genre that is more than music—it’s movement, identity, and soul. Instantly, bodies rise. Feet hit the floor. Smiles spread. It’s impossible to stay still when those drums and layered rhythms take over. Every track invites movement—not just any dance, but movements deeply rooted in tradition. Fast-paced footwork, shoulders bouncing in rhythm, and smooth, controlled waist whining evoke the spirit of ceremonies, weddings, street parties, and everyday joy back home. Traditional celebratory calls—ululations, chants, and shout-outs—echo across the room, uniting everyone under one shared beat, no matter where in the diaspora we may be. Afrobeats is not just music you hear. It’s music you feel.

Taking off my headphones after I finished listening to my pieces. Close my eyes and concentrate on what’s around me: and it’s an air machine. It’s always some air machine, it seems like, or a fan, or some temperature regulator, or something’s exhaust. Are they everywhere? Maybe it’s good I’m noticing them (instead of silence), but how do I move past them? What’s beyond the ventilation system? What’s in it? Sssssnnnillilsrrrssssh.Those are my nostrils. That’s me. I guess it ventilates too, and it makes noise. What’s up with the different sound timescales? Where’s the great orderly fugue of air machines?

No matter day or night, no matter if you are awake or asleep, the air purifier in the room is always up and running. It’s so consistent that you forget about its existence, its constant whoofing. Sound that inhales and exhales in the room. But if you turn it off, it all of a sudden gets too quiet, quiet to the point where it feels eerily awkward, like those times when the entire class just stops talking altogether and everyone looks at each other as if something was going to happen.

Low drone, just bass. I can feel something emerging in my gut, then tearing through the fabric of the sky. A higher drone enters as pitch rises, a point of clarity, then reverse, pitch decreases, the high drone fades away, the low drone returns then sinks into my belly. Did that dude really eat a plane?

I struggle to wake up in the morning. Lying in bed, my alarm goes off. It’s a twinkling sound which begins slowly and crescendos into a persistent chime. I instinctively turn it off and set a five-minute timer. In a blink, that goes off too. My phone is lost somewhere; the chiming is muffled by my covers. I find it after digging through my blankets - this process repeats several more times before I eventually leave bed.

Ambience is often underappreciated. Maybe that’s a lie. Nowadays, I think people recognize the role ambience can play in pretty much anything. It can set the tone in a certain room: bustling and rhythmic during a family get together. It can be slow, calculated, and dark in a horror movie or videogame, making you sit anxiously in near silence, anticipating a jump scare at any moment. It can even be a repetitive, monotonous sound, one you likely often hear but never pay attention to, like the hum of a car engine warming up during cold season. Ambience is a sound that in general, you don’t really listen to. But, when you do truly listen, it makes all the difference.

Tropical instruments. The land is dug by a mushroom. The low ends are the texture of raw salmon. Persistent wub, just one. half the ears on top of the water, half the ears under. There are light engine sounds, chains turning, rattling. on the very top of all things you have reverberating keys that remind of the cold plastic that used to coat their keyboards. Largeness.

Clink! Clink! Plink! Eyelids, blink blink blink from plaster baskets along the wall. Subtle, acoustic happenstance. Timing designed visually. One eye to one basket being: blink blink blink. Plink! Clink! Clink, plink! An orchestra of uncoordinated watchers, always peering, never sleeping. More clink! when small; more plink! when long. The sounds are defined by the hollow impressions of weave and weft topography left by the basket ghosts.
Gusts of painterly unidirectional wind, twinkly tap tap, woosh woosh, twinkly tap tap. A more distant but louder, angrier, and anguished circular, stormy pink noise. Do it all again.

Title (no article): Another Constant Sound in the Background
Full Title: Another Constant Sound in the Background
Journal Entry: The birds chirping, heard constantly throughout the whole video. Another constant sound in the background is what would be traffic or cars going by. A voice in the background within the first 6 seconds. A constant pop or thump followed by smoother sound (snap), earthy. The first presence of the audio includes both nature and city soundscapes. Both settings are intertwined. The birds chirp while there is a low rumble of cars passing by. Calm but busy. It feels as if these two sounds play the main role, meaning they feel closer to the listener. We hear this thump, a sound that expresses something making contact with another thing. The thump is followed by a snap, a harsh but then pleasant snap. A voice in the distance appears after the first. The repetition of the thump and snap proceed, but each with a different level or smooth and roughness. There are levels to this sound. Some feel closer to you while others are heard from afar.

There is a constant chorus of crickets chirping in the background. The first new entrant is a bird singing a song with an initial high note, and then three repeated triplets. A different bird sings a song of muted laughter as a car calmly accelerates by. You hear the footsteps of the recorder for the first time as they crunch dry leaves with their step. A third bird enters with a song that is similar to a typical chip but has the quality of a bouncing ball that gradually repeats quicker and quicker before ending.

The gondola creaks through the Swiss alps as it latches onto the cable, jerking slightly before gliding smoothly upwards with a steady hum. Through the cracks in the windows the wind whistles as ghostly breath against the silence of the alpine expanse. Below, the snow acts as an earmuff to the world by softly absorbing the shouts of skiers carving fresh lines in the powder. Each tower approached is an equal distance apart, interrupting the steady glide with a brief, jittering tremor. As the wheels grip the metal framework, a deep resonant thunk reverberates through the cabin.

Tinkling is the flowing fabric, metal film sewn like a fish’s scales. Faint tune was descending from the ground while dancers ascended the staircase. The space in which we hold the traveling sound is summoning a traveler’s boat. Tinkling, dangling, swaying, the fish scales play themselves an isolating song.

Late night silence, TV colors flashing on faces. Cool breeze from the window. But, a slow baseline, quiet anticipation buzzes from the televised crowd. Anticipation from us in the living room, warm light not quite matching the dark scene on the TV. Music slowing, beats of silence, rustling. Leaning forward, getting closer to the broadcast of a song we know so well. Quiet. Quiet there and here. The best part is coming. And suddenly, bass eruption, kick drums, desperation turned to electric guitar powerhouse. Late night silence turned electric.

I twist in a winding motion as my hand presses against my knee. The shifting of my vertebrae echoes up to my skull with a cacophony of cracks. However, they are irregular and abruptly stop, leaving me second-guessing whether something else is waiting to be released.
Soprano screeeeching in the key of almost-F, reaching a higher-pitched apex when an obstructive piece of conifer penetrates a previously undisturbed brown noise of motion.

Take your mark. Get Set. POW. A combo heard countless times. Each moment shortening in words, building your anxiety. That gunshot bursting before you do. As soon as you hear it, you hear nothing else. The sound of a race is one of silence for me. Once that shot is fired, it cuts everything out like putting hearing muffs on. Funny how the loudest and most violent sound is the last thing you hear until you cross that line.

Low electric buzzing fills the room as the clippers glide steadily along the back of my head. Soft snips of scissors punctuate the air, quick and precise, followed by the faint whisper of loose hair falling onto the floor. The barber’s shoes shuffle lightly against the tile while the chair creaks and swivels in small adjustments. A quiet, steady hum of fluorescent lights hangs overhead, broken only by the occasional brush of a broom sweeping scattered hair aside.
A horse with an erratic, awkward, fast-then-slow walking pattern is wearing rubber horseshoes and being corralled in a circle, while berated by both trash talk and celebratory “woo!”s.

A basketball in a gym does not just bounce, it detonates in short rubber bursts that return from the walls half a second later. Sneakers add squeaks that skate over the wood, high and thin against the heavier drum of the ball. The whole soundscape is made of impact, friction, and echo, athletic movement translated into acoustics.

A swift rip. Paper tearing. A dry sound standing in contrast to the wet drip of the faucet, plunking into the contents of the clogged sink. A mechanical whirring, somewhere between high-pitched and low. It reminds me of a recently resurfaced video from the depths of the internet of a goat screaming. AHHHH. Paper dispensing like a tongue.

It feels too early and too human for this. Sounds of man and machine right outside my open window. Even if I close my eyes and cover myself with blankets there is still a hum, a vibration, a quaking of labor rattling at the windows.

Title (no article): Berkshire Regional Transit Authority (BRTA) Shuttle to Walmart - North Adams
Full Title: The Berkshire Regional Transit Authority (BRTA) Shuttle to Walmart - North Adams
Journal Entry: I pull my student ID from my pocket, the plastic whispering against cloth. I show it, and the moment passes quietly between me and the driver. Then I step into the bus, into a moving room of soft noise–engine humming, bags shifting, old people’s voices low like something distant. Suddenly, a voice rises above it all, clear and steady: “BRTA now approaching Proprietor Street…” It returns again and again, like a clock made of sound. “BRTA now approaching Stop&Shop…”  “BRTA now approaching Main Street…” The bus carries us forward, and everything moves in rhythm. The brakes sigh, the windows tremble slightly, the road speaks beneath the wheels. No one says much, yet we are all inside the same sound. The voice keeps announcing, naming places as we pass them, turning the journey into a series of spoken markers. Time is measured not in minutes, but in stops.

The violins whimsically hop around like bunnies. The alto saxophone, smooth like butter, glides softly around the hall. The trombone’s notes are playing and my heartbeat aligns with their rhythm.  A metal rod is being banged in a frightening ominous tempo.
The violins intensify and crescendo so high we reach a blue sky above. They take me for a ride, flying through the clouds. The walls echo hundreds of years of human nature and history. The love in the harmonies, fear of the low sounds, anticipation of the crescendo, and life’s grandness as the orchestra came together in a sweeping of perfection that swelled my eyes with tears and the soundwaves from the cymbal sending chills that are rushing through my body and surrounding Chapin Hall.

Every morning, when I leave Susie Hopkins House out of the side door, a bird flaps above my head. She has nested just above the fire door, and never fails to be startled by my arrival. She used to startle me, too; the rapid thwaping of her wings would make me flinch. Now, I open the door as slowly as possible.

Title (no article): Bird Heard Living Beneath Tented Roofs of Hollander Hall
Full Title: Bird Heard Living Beneath Tented Roofs of Hollander Hall
Journal Entry: A rubber duck squeaks through birdsong, candy rocks colliding. The bird snaps and bounces and spins and screeches screeches in highest pitch. It made all of these sounds. When it was not screeching, the rubbery noises can be heard like a laundrywoman squeezing, rinsing.

Cold air, the stadium lights humming high above the track, the crowd murmuring behind us like the ocean far away. Eight bodies settle into the blocks, spikes scraping metal, then a silence so tight you can hear someone swallow two lanes over. “Set.” The whole stadium holds its breath, hips rise, muscles coil. Then the gun cracks the night open, and the silence shatters into a storm of spikes tearing at the rubber, sharp like rain on a tin roof, the crowd roaring back to life. Ten seconds of thunder, then the finish line, and the quiet comes rushing back.

High shrills. Deep resonant a’s and h’s. Soft spoken. Timid shaky voices dripping with such sweetness. Rustling of bulky fabric rubbing against fabric. The hollow rattling of several plastic buckets rings out. Hard bangs against plastic. Quick clicks. Crinkle of wrappers. So many of these sounds layered upon each other. Some buckets have more hard bangs. Others have more clicks. I can guess what kind of candy is in each person's buckets and how much. Shaking mine, I only hear the muffled crinkles of wrappers.

BoOOOOOom, PoOOOOOw, ZooOOOOm. When you walk out the art studio with the Boom Microphone that's all you hear as each car races down the road. As you walk up towards Driscoll, you hear laughter and giggles from the practices going on.  The closer you point the microphone, the more intense it gets.

Do we need to break it - no it’s only in your head. The real house is fine - shingles. We fall slowly. Sound of bright clay turned into stone, crisp rock strike ones, but without the deep lurking background of air when you’re inside. air now. The people talking. You are like a locust. buzz of street life, prayer songs.. you glide and slice into ceramic tiles. the sound of creamy keyboard clicks and dropped hard glass vases spinning on the floor, a rich, delicate reckoning. hard but never harsh. The patterns make it musical. What is more musical, the short, never reverberated clicks of copper, not unlike the vile sound of plastic in its lack of depth, but nonetheless a distinct cupric flavor, like hitting an empty jug, like knocking on a cast iron gate, without the deep part. Everything you do outside that door is without the deep part. claques of the floor.

Sometimes it sticks to the roof of my mouth, snags on the obstructions that are the body to create the pitch of its movement. Faster intakes through a nearly closed mouth are higher-pitched, sounding rushed. Almost a whistle. Almost music. Through the nose, the sound is textured. Muffled, sounding blurred but more audible. With further obstruction and more interference comes more sound. Odd shapes made with wrangled tongues shape the noise air releases. Strange lip postures and air sucked in through teeth hiss and whistle like wind. Silent calm breaths rock no waves; harsh exhales transport emotions to ears. Breath is always sounding. How often do we hear it?

Lifting the plastic container creates a rubbing sound like two balloons rubbing together, a plasticy bumping of the elbows as the pourer’s skin comes into contact with the handle. The pouring motion is fairly quiet in terms of the plastic, so we can clearly hear the stream of water coming out of the spout and landing first deeply, then shallowly, in a water bottle as it fills. The friction between the plastic and other surfaces returns as we place the pitcher back on the table, and it comes to rest.

ZZZZZZZZZZZZZZ. A sound that makes me smack every inch of my face. The heavy loudness created by such a small insect will never cease to surprise me. The fading sound of the fly’s buzz haunts me, as I know that it’ll only be followed by the chaotic sharpness of the fly’s wing as it runs away from me. I hear the changing in frequency as the fly flies up and down, meaning that it’s putting up a fight to escape me. I lie awake, haunted by the eeriness of its buzz. I heard its loud snap after my father held this large creature in his hands, only to learn that it wasn’t dead yet.

Bzzzzt-bzzzt against the wooden table when I’m sleeping is almost as loud as a ringtone in class. It sounds like a bumblebee trapped under a cup. Then follows the kiki sound if it’s an alarm. That’s when you have to decide within a second whether to snooze it or get up. If it happens to be a suppressed notification while you’re at the table, it sends the message into every resting elbow. If the ear won’t listen, the body will.

My grandmother’s voice has always been firm yet kind. Although we are separated by the vast expanse of the Pacific Ocean, with the help of modern technology, we can still hear each other’s voices. That is through WeChat calls. Her voice may be “rough,” just like the mild land, but to me it is truly gentle and full of nostalgia. The trace of local dialect in her accent only makes it feel all the more familiar. Perhaps this is the power of the human voice—it connects people.

Title (no article): Caught in a 2am Rain While Studying Late in the DC Center
Full Title: Caught in a 2am Rain While Studying Late in the DC Center
Journal Entry: It is 2am when I step out of the DC Center. The door opens, and the sound hits me first– rain, heavy and constant. It fills everything. I pause for a second, listening, then step into it. The rain lands on the ground, on rooftops, on my clothes, each drop adding to the noise. As I walk, my footsteps mix with the water. My shoes press into wet pavement, soft and uneven. Cars pass in the distance, their tires cutting through puddles. The rain does not stop or change, it surrounds me completely. I am inside it, moving through a world made only of water and sound.

Graw graw graw gnaw gnaw gnaw crunch crunch cruch the juices swooshes between my teeth as they grind the stick. Shhhhhhhhh pressure increase as the strand lengthens and snaps! To curl and into a silent coil.

It stutters at first, but then a high squeak pierces through the room. I shudder. It settles a raspy and dry rhythm as it moves across the board. However, just when I think I can relax, another sharp screech makes me shudder again.

In the middle of campus you hear it every fifteen minutes or so, just like how you would imagine a giant bell sound. It is annoying sometimes and pleasant sometimes, depending on what it reminds me of, lunch or gym.

The crisp crunch of ice sounds like the crackle of a bag of chips. As I listen to the crunchy noises of ice as I break down large pieces of ice, my mind tastes the saltiness of a bag of Lay’s chips. The sharp sound of flavorless water breaking through the air tastes good. Schtoch, snap, crack, kkchosht. The salty sound of chewing ice slicing through the air, through every bite, evokes hunger.

La la la la la la la la la la la la la…The birds chirp, chirp chirp chirp. The smile on my face sounds louder than any surrounding chatter. In my own world, step, step step. The squeak of stone below me graced with an evening dew perhaps rain.

There are no specific times during the day where the cicadas in Shanghai will start making their noise, but for me, it is usually a lazy afternoon as you lay in your bedroom after lunch. A few cicadas will first periodically make some sound, but that’s normal and expected in the summer. But then there will be a certain time, probably a few minutes, where more and more cicadas join, and the sound gets exponentially louder. The sound would eventually become unbearable as it penetrates through the wall and windows, loud enough to the point where it makes you stop whatever you’re doing and look outside the window, trying to locate where it's coming from, but it's everywhere. I can’t find a single cicada, even though my window is right next to a tree.

The vacuum roars through each room, swallowing dust with a harsh mechanical growl that drowns out everything else. Spray bottles snap and hiss, sending sharp bursts of cleaner across glass and countertops. Rags scrape in fast circular motions while drawers open, slam, and shuffle with the movement of forgotten objects. The apartment fills with the sound of labor and renewal, chaotic at first, then gradually cleaner and quieter.

Be mindful of your tone, your pitch, being presentable, and your vocabulary. There’s a language filled with a history frowned upon by the gatekeepers of opportunity. That language is not safe to use outside of communities that look like me. Laughter that’s so resonant, that originates from our core, is so hard to keep in that we fall off our chairs, clap randomly, and run out of the room. Slang that only we understand, accompanied by our accents, is a language of peace amongst ourselves, but a symbol of poverty to the outside. I watch individuals who look like me greet me with African American Vernacular English and quickly quiet their voices, adjust their tone of speech, and completely bury the person who just greeted me, desperate to be valued. A language that withstands centuries but must be used in a timely fashion.

The day is so long. They pray for coffee. They chant a ritualistic call for coffee, syllable fragmented, sound dispersed. Words are chopped down and elongated yet the calling is flowing onward. Coffee. They pray for coffee. The day is so long. The day is too long so it sounds like their voices are tuned wrong. Are these distant calls from the old times or really does time travel and suddenly it is today. Surreal, bizarre, no arrangement, voices falling apart. They pray for coffee. The pitch starts low and the desire sounds heavy. The desire explodes. A high pitch call followed by a spacious chorus voice. When words are no longer murmuring but distinguishable, we hear everything, every piece of request and chattering. We get too close so it all ends at that moment.

I really like the sound of the coffee maker’s bloop bloop bloop. Bubbles that rise from the bottom to the top, surfacing and disappearing. Some are long, some are short. But they make silly sounds. If you blur your eyes, it could be early in the morning when the tile is cold and the mourning doves echo. bllooop bloop bllooop. It could be late at night, when only the living room light is on. bllink bloorp, little ticks, It’s almost as though the o’s travel upwards too, onomatopoeia.

It’s a Nalgene. The ridged wheel clicks and bounces against the wall of the bottle-friendly station before it goes still, hanging by its flat, plastic thread. Shrp. A little sip, so I can fill it up more. No metallic taste because there’s a nice filter on the bottle-friendly station. Clmp clmp clmp. Twist on, breath. Ah. Walk on. Cold water drips down fingers. Shake it off, smack.

Dry gravel crunches sharply beneath each step, the sound unnaturally loud in the midnight stillness. A cold wind threads through the stone markers, stirring leaves into faint, papery whispers that scrape across the ground. Somewhere in the distance, branches creak and sway like tired hinges, followed by the sudden snap of a twig in the dark. Long stretches of silence press heavily between each noise, making every small sound feel watchful and alive.

The tip of a tongue poised to spit out a word. The shudder in a hand that reaches through the dark to touch something. The hollow of an empty candy wrapper, curling around an absence. The wings of a bird rising up at the end of a swoop just before it lands.

The melody of the instruments coming together leaves you in awe. One song after another, my ears were clapping and singing with happiness. At the end, the crowd clapped and screamed, showing their appreciation for everything

I’m at a concert with my friend, far from home. This is the first time I’ve gotten to see this singer live. He’s from my home, he’s also queer. The song, originally devotional, remains devotional, even when far removed from its history—devotional to hope, community, love, queerness, home. It’s the same verse over and over again. Originally about a groom, the beloved becomes genderless here in a way, both bride and groom. The language remains the same but its tone and texture keep changing: unsynced claps from the audience; someone coughs; a consistent sound of underlying instruments in the background. There’s commentary added too: it’s a congregation; it’s a wedding/shadi in Manhattan; it’s queer, it’s joyful, it’s togetherness.

You asked me what cool water sounds like when I pour it into a cup. Hot water? Now I am sitting by the river. It sounds hurried. The water streams by in huge quantities that you can hear. You can hear it stretching away, higher, and higher. It is loud. So loud, that listening to it, the cold leeches out through your ears to the rest of your body. Cold, Ice Blue, Green. Light but deep at the same time. Where does this color come from? Does it come from the temperature, from the cold? Can you see the temperature in the color of the water? It looks like the color of huge tons of ice. Snowmelt. Can you see the snow in the color of the water? Can you hear it? Glaciers? Snowflakes? Ice frozen into cracks in the road?

I slowly sink into my bed, being swallowed by dirty sheets and the thick air of the room. I stayed there for hours. I stay there so long that it becomes a performance against the natural functions of the body. I hear my bladder tighten and my legs squeeze close as they try to hold in urine. I hear my belly gurgle in a low pitch scream as it begs for sustenance. I hear my saliva change viscosity craving a cigarette.

Your toes land on the carpeted stair, causing the wood beneath to begin to ache under your weight. As you flatten your foot, applying more pressure to the old structure, pops of cracking and shifting explode and then soon subside once you are at equilibrium. Once you begin to lift your foot, the built-up tension bursts once more in an eruptive creek as the wood shifts back into place.
