In the field behind my dorm, they squeak, ree-ree-ree-ree-ree-ree, as if to find the loudest among them or catch human attention. Yet when you approach, trying to pick just one, it goes mute. When you walk past, it resumes loud again, and the one right at your feet stops. So you are basically walking in a bubble of silence amidst a cricket screaming competition.

The crosswalk signal clicks in an even pulse, a dry synthetic tapping that organizes bodies at the curb. It is less a voice than a command translated into rhythm, designed to be legible in traffic and weather. Heard closely, it sounds almost insect-like, but in the city it functions as public instruction.

Soon after the last crumb was pecked by the morning bird, I realized that the bird’s hunger never ceased. In this position I now found myself as a servant to the morning birds. Because they eat in the morning this meant that my routine now revolved around their eating schedule. Every morning, I woke up at 4am, to collect the crumbs. I would crawl on the floor searching meticulously in the fibers of the carpet with a magnified glass. When the sun rose at 6:30am I had to be quick to feed the birds hungry beaks, otherwise I feared that they may eat me. They hunger was relentless, and as a result I grew weaker, yet scraping by just enough to satisfy their bellies.

It didn’t used to happen, but now I brace for the abrasive sound. It’s jarring, something you know shouldn’t be there. Worrisome, a problem. Turning the key makes it sound like something hard is gnashing against a zipper. Maybe even almost sounds like a zipper. It’s quick, but leaves its residue of unappealing sound in my head. Maybe in my body too, the reverberations feel like nails on a chalkboard. I should really tell her to get her car checked out.

My inner voice is calling out—I finally have a plot of my own to grow flowers! As I wander among the plots, the wood chips beneath my feet rub together, occasionally snapping with soft cracks. When I water the soil, bubbles rise up—that’s the sound of the earth drinking in the moisture. Even the sound of digging while planting is pleasing to the ear. New sprouts seem to tell the spring breeze about their vibrant vitality, and I can almost hear these little seedlings growing. I look forward to it—so much!

Splash, rushhh, plunk, hisss, plop. It’s a mix of splashes and low tumbling rumbles when the current hits the rocks. The water slaps against the stone with a rhythmic plop. There’s an underlying rush that gives the sense of momentum and weight. A louder splash breaks through as the water shifts or pushes. You can feel its restlessness. You can feel its natural power.

A low whir begins as soon as one’s foot strikes the belt. The whir grows into growl as your legs move faster. Beneath it all is the steady, rhythmic pounding of each step, echoing strangely against the curve. The growl slows back into a whirl and the eventually stillness. Until the next person steps on.

It initiated from a small cracking sound, then suddenly a loud explosion. I entered the crack, with smoke surrounding me and blocking my view. It was a maze that trains, castles and soldiers were working and operating. The beaming of the train, the rubbing of the helmets, and the bell ringing in the castles all embrace my ear. The sound is becoming more and more intense that makes me feel dizzy and unable to even stand still. I urgently traveled in the maze trying to find a way out, until the operating world was upside down. It was not until the next day that I passed by the window of the Williams shop that I realized my reflection on the window is pointing to a tiny world made by models.

It should be silent, only the rustling of paper, the scratching of lead. Pausing, and erasing, and scratching again, the only thing that should fill the room. And yet, there is a lawn mower, a leaf blower, a Dr. Seuss parade if it were all condensed into one continuous rumbling sound, outside the window. As if it’s passing back and forth right beside the classroom, trying to find an opening to disrupt what little focus already exists. When it finally ends, this horribly cacophonous interruption, there is bliss. A sweet silence, quickly followed by an oppressive silence. Any movement, squeaky water bottle, cough, or tapping echoes across the room. And it begins again.

Ding Dong. “Hello there, I like your costume. Can I get a picture?” Those were the words from Maud Mandel as I entered her home for Halloween. The floors creaked as I walked towards the candy basket. I knew I was in for more surprises. The only problem was, I didn’t know when it would come. As I put my hand in the candy basket and grabbed my snickers bar, out of nowhere a hand popped out. “Ohhhh shit.”  The air then proceeded to be filled with laughter.

Morning, and the dining hall is just waking up, trays sliding onto metal rails with a hollow, scraping clatter. The waffle iron hisses as batter hits the hot plate, then beeps three times when it’s done, sharp and impatient. Silverware clinks against plates in every corner, a messy rhythm with no beat, like wind chimes in a storm. Voices rise and fall in low, sleepy waves, broken by a laugh that bursts out and fades just as fast. Behind it all, the dish return belt rumbles steadily, carrying the clinks and clatters away until the room empties back into a quiet hum.

I put my tray on the belt and it just leaves. It rattles off into the dark hole in the wall: kshhk-kshhk-tink. Forks and knives are being thrown onto a pile sitting by the belt. Behind the wall is a whole different world. Spraying, a hiss like a car wash, metal racks slamming, etc. I’ve eaten there for a whole year, and I have never seen back there. I only know it by sound, and well so.

Rhythmic waves hit the outer wall of the dishwasher. They come in a pattern of repeated doubles muffled by the barrier of plastic and metal that contains the chaotic yet methodical cleansing. This cycle continues over and over with the water returning to the wall in what seems like a circular motion, ultimately subsiding, but only for a moment before starting up again.

Sticky fingers unsticking from a sticky object. Tic-tica, tic-ti-tac. Hard candy skittering across the floor, getting stuck somewhere unseen in a crack behind, or underneath. That one floorboard in the hallway that groans even when no one’s walking on it. Waiting on the platform for a train that never comes, only the ones in the other direction.

Hollow, Metallic, Resonant, Metronomic, Elastic. Rope clangs relentlessly against a tall, hollow metal pole, far up above the quad valley. It’s intermittent, as if autonomic, giving up as the wind winds down. It’s alive, it seems… Down the pole, a faint dripping, inside and out, like drops pinging off the walls of a distant room.

The tiles go under our hands first, dragged in slow circles across the board, a dry gravel churn, the sound of many hands agreeing. Then the slam. One crack, bone on plank, and the whole table answers, the hollow under it swelling the hit into something the size of a gunshot down the road. The next one lands louder. Nothing in the game asks for this; it is only the yard telling the street it is full.
Click, click, rum dilldi rum dilldi rom dilldi rum dilldi rom dilldi rum……boink. Fallalalalalalalalala

The persistent humming of a desk fan increases and decreases in intensity as it oscillates. An extension cord wines, ramping up in pitch before subsiding. There is something else in the background, faint, hiding behind the intensity of the larger fan; it is the quiet spinning of an air purifier from the corner of the room. The extension cord’s wine returns once more, before quickly going back into hiding.

The plump weight of silence in bright sunlight. A white rabbit the shape of a child, swinging on a swing who silence smells like damp mown grass drying where morning meets afternoon. The birthday cake textured silence of a small white house with red shutters open on the windows. The rabbit-child’s scream is silent the way the light holds its breath, the sky smothers a blue belly laugh, a spiderweb clings to its last drop of dew.

Too rhythmic and not at all, if I squeeze my eyes shut, the chirps and drones and hums and croaks will overwhelm me. Where one stops another begins a cacophony from critters almost too far to hear, at my feet a leaf falls with a satisfying crunch.

Title (no article): Dropping My Ear in the Great Barrier Reef
Full Title: Dropping My Ear in the Great Barrier Reef
Journal Entry: The sounds produced by coral are layered. Starting from the surface, there are living coral polyps, whose sticky sounds are the result of microscopic tentacles contracting and expanding. The growth of algae and the reproduction of various organisms all produce audible sounds to communicate with each other. Diving deeper, the calcium carbonate skeletons of coral emit the sounds of chemical reactions, transmitting toward the surface. These are resonanting, yet full of vitality, as the coral reef itself is a vast living organism. Continuing to descend, I feel as if I can hear the entire reef breathing, which is both ancient yet vibrant at the same time.A loud explosion shattered my listening, which is the sound of a fishing boat’s horn. The propeller was racing across the surface of the coral reef, carrying my listening far away.

The speakers rumbled loudly, blasting a mix of drums, bass, vocals, and backing tracks through the air, loud enough that I felt the vibrations in my body. A low hum, barely audible, resonated on my right as hundreds of drones floated high in the air above me. Almost a hundred thousand voices echoed across the stadium, all slightly off key but combining to match the singer perfectly. Pianos, Synths, Bass, Drums, they all played in key, mixed to perfection and almost shouting at me from the speakers. These are all the sounds I heard at the drum show.

Click, Clap, Snap, Whir, Cluck. The shutter and mirror move as you take a photo. The click of the mirror popping up. Your finger hits the target, creating a quick “click” as the shutter opens and closes. The change in setting to autofocus makes a subtle whirring sound as the lens motor adjusts to find focus.

It’s 5 in the morning in early May. I’ve spent the past night in the 24-hour room, and I’ve taken a break for this all-nighter ritual: see the sunrise and hear the birds sing. I can’t describe it as chirping or tweeting. It sounds like running your fingers through warm sand. The wind in your ears—everything is waking up.

Peace, garbage, whoosh. It’s almost like a small town, empty, but only for a second. Rising energy, the concrete stretches as it gets brushed and swept of its litter. Those up probably see it all, the fall and the rise, day after day. Quiet, very quiet, with a warm fuzz.

Crunch, Snap Munch, Gulp. There is a satisfying crunch when you bite into its crisp skin. The outside texture is firm but once the teeth have used its strength to break it down, the juiciness of the flesh releases a sweet or tart flavor (depending on the type of apple). The crisp, sharp crunch is the most dominant sound, often echoing with a snap. The juice creates a soft liquid like noise.

Velcro straps ripped apart. The sound of many neurons firing at once. Prrrrrrrrbbbbbttttt. Hissings fades in and dominates as soon as they tire. If you tap the electrode, you’ll hear a pop. A spike on the monitor will appear. Tk. Tk. Ftttttttttttttt You sit and wait. Will it sing?
Shoes off, toes flick and rub under wool socks. Ft. Ft. If you stomp with shoes on, or kick your wheely chair to roll yourself away, the electrode will surge. False data. It’s better to sit, silently, and wait, listening to the fuzz of the amplifier.

It’s louder this time. More insistent. Do machines change their tone when they get upset? It’s behind me, panting like a dog in a hot, wet room. It reminds me I’m being surveilled. The sound of sleep on an airplane, miles passing quickly in the empty air beneath.

The low hum of the espresso machine swells and recedes, a steady undercurrent to the staccato bursts of steam hissing through milk. Ceramic cups clink against saucers, their crisp chime punctuating the rhythmic murmur of conversation, voices rising and falling like the tide. A door swings open with a breath of cold air, the outside world rushing in for just a moment before settling back into the warm cocoon of coffee and sound.

Home spills through the phone speaker as a layered tangle of sound. Voices stack on top of each other: bright, mid-pitched laughter, the shrill sparks of children cutting through, someone’s deeper voice rolling underneath like a steady drum. It’s a living cacophony—messy, overlapping, impossible to untangle, and so, so far away.
Swoosh…very quiet sound. It’s the sound of drawing the medication from the vial. Quiet pop sound. The sound of pulling out the needle from the vial.

The van groans steadily down the road, its engine humming low beneath the constant rattle of loose panels and shifting bags. Tires thud over cracks and potholes, jolting the cabin in uneven waves that make sleeping bodies sway against windows and one another. Heavy breathing and faint snores rise from every seat, layered into a drowsy chorus of exhaustion. Occasionally, someone stirs, fabric rustles, then the vehicle settles back into its long mechanical drone.

Fall is a reflective season. The weather is cool, but not freezing. The leaves are colorful, the ones on the ground are crunchy. It seems like a quiet season, but sound is unavoidable. The environment makes it a perfect time to think, even if there’s nothing in particular to think about. The river is flowing, the sun is shining, and the birds chirp monotonously. The leaves are crunchy, and the pinecones are crunchier.

Afternoon light, low and golden, and the air smells like cold apples and smoke. Leaves let go one by one, ticking against branches in a soft papery rattle, while each step crunches loud and dry, like stepping on cereal. The wind picks up and the whole tree exhales at once, a rushing hiss that sends leaves skittering across the sidewalk like small animals running for cover. Across the quad, students kick through a pile, laughter bouncing off the buildings as leaves burst into the air with a crisp, crackling roar and rain back down in a dry shower. Then the wind settles, the voices drift off toward class, and the leaves go back to whispering as the day starts to cool.

Title (no article): Fanfare of the 20th Century Fox Is a Sound of Arrival
Full Title: The Fanfare of the 20th Century Fox Is a Sound of Arrival
Journal Entry:
It is a bold announcement.
It builds anticipation.
It feels like a curtain slowly rising before a show begins.
It gathers everyone’s attention.
It asks for silence.
It creates expectation.
In a few seconds, it turns an ordinary room into a theater.
The trumpets open wide, filling the air.
The notes do not hurry - they stand strong and proud.
Each phrase lands clearly, like a spotlight clicking on.
There is space between the lines -
not empty silence, but suspense.
Then the sound grows fuller -
horns layered together, rich and golden.
A final bright note rings out
and lingers for a breath
before fading into waiting.
The sound rises upward.
It feels tall, like pillars made of music.
It makes the moment bigger.
It makes what comes next feel important -
Cinematic, and meant to happen.

The sound of good posture. A pinch in the lower back, chest fills with air, and that one little problem spot in the left shoulder pipes up again. Imagine doing cat-cow, sitting up. There’s no squeak of plastic foam under the knees, but the almost imperceptible, high-pitched zings of fascia separating are audible — gone almost instantly. Can you hear separation? No one else can hear what I do. Only if I really crack my back.

Title (no article): Five Men Near and on Swings
Full Title: Five Men Near and on Swings
Journal Entry: Boisterous echoes of collective bursts traveling from here to there, taking up space with organic, geological reflections and inflections. The distant quieted voices sound quarterback-ly or backwards-hat-ful. Ungreased chains squeak at a rhythmic, pitchy, songbird call, while outpaced by sporadic bursts of laughter that travel with the deep, low intensity of a whale call.

Rustle, whisper, soft, hushed, crackle. As the pages lift, there is a soft flutter. On release the pages emit a hushed rustle. It is thin but crisp. The pages then settle into a faint whisper of a distant crackle.
A soft rattle emits from its bean filled belly as I would hug it close at night. Its limbs make gentle plops as they fall against my quilted blanket. A feeling of comfort and safety wraps over me.

The fluorescent lights produce a faint electric buzz that disappears only when I deliberately lean toward it. Once noticed, it becomes impossible to unhear, a narrow band of sound stretched above the room like wire. It marks the classroom as a space powered into being, its quietness held together by current.

The coffee shop collapses into a hush. Rustling fabric against headphones, the most prominent sound. A chair drags across the floor three tables away, gritty, its edge blunted by foam and distance. Somewhere behind me, a jacket zipper chatters twice, metal striking, a bright little clash. Milk froths in short, distant bursts. Beneath, conversation moves in soft currents: vowels and consonants dissolved, a continuous murmur that has the shape of language but none of its meaning. All of it reaches me softened and rounded.

The sound of footsteps gathers shape as it moves closer to me, growing brighter, more defined, until it is directly outside my door. For a second, the rhythm feels suspended at my threshold, hovering in the space between hallway and room, then it begins to recede, each step swallowed inch by inch by the corridor. Silence barely settles before another presence pulls itself forward from the far end: slower, heavier, a dragging scuff that combs against the carpet with a tired insistence. I hear the friction, textured and uneven, until it passes my door at its fullest. Then it, too, diminishes, the drag smoothing into a distant hush, leaving behind only the impression of movement.

A fork scraping a plate produces a thin, bright scream that cuts through every other sound at the table. It is brief but impossible to ignore, because its frequency sits where the ear feels immediately defensive. As a cultural sound, it carries instant discomfort, the body learning to recoil before thought has time to form.

Click click clack, achoooo, rustling of overstuffed backpack, shuffling of feet against felt-like flooring, achooo (deeper), slidee into desk, zipppppp, clicks with urgencies, door, the loudest possible creaking of an ergonomic office chair which trains you to sit in it the least ergonomically, water bottle sip, water bottle settles on desk, *sigh* underlined by the sighlence and HVAC white—or maybe pink—noise.

Crisp, authentic, joyful, energetic. This audio was recorded at a Galentine’s event hosted by Sisterhood, a campus club dedicated to uniting Black women. The recording captures the essence of our gathering—joyous laughter rippling through the room, conversations weaving between reflections on long weeks, and the celebratory exclamations of “Flaunt it!” as we acknowledged making it through another week at Williams College. The energy in the space was undeniable. Our voices—animated, warm, and unguarded—created a fullness that resonated throughout the room, a testament to the deep comfort of being in community. There was excitement in finally coming together, but also a collective exhale, a shared relief in being able to drop our defenses and just be. A powerful theme emerged when we asked, “What does love mean to you?” While some hesitated, searching for the right words through thoughtful pauses, murmured “umms,” and quiet “I don’t knows,” a common thread surfaced: love, at its core, is sacrifice. Whether through actions, words, or unspoken gestures, love—true, deep, and unwavering—was understood as a willingness to give of oneself for the people who matter most. This theme underscored the essence of Sisterhood itself, a space built on the sacrifice of time, energy, and care to uplift and hold each other in love.

GOALLLLL. On the home side of the bleachers, the fans were roaring with joy and excitement, happy that they scored. On the opposite side of the bleachers, the Middlebury fans were silent, you could hear a pin drop. As I maneuver myself through the wet grass and mud of the soccer pitch, the game grows more and more intense.

Title (no article): Going to the Flower Market with My Parents
Full Title: Going to the Flower Market with My Parents
Journal Entry: It was the first place where I truly felt life, color, and liveliness through sound. Plants cannot speak, yet when I heard people discussing how to grow them, it felt as if they were communicating with the plants themselves. The sunlight pouring down from the greenhouse roof had a warmth that felt almost audible. The sound of the faucet turning on meant that a “shower” was about to fall. All of this was thanks to the radiant, shimmering version of myself wandering through the flower market. I allowed my life to connect with nature, but now most of those markets have closed, as if certain doors in my life had been gently shut. How I miss those sounds that carried my childhood. Perhaps this also means I am slowly becoming capable of standing on my own, able to face the regrets that time inevitably presses forward.

The river does not stop speaking. Water moves over stone, breaking, gathering, falling again. It never repeats the same way twice, yet it feels steady, like a living rhythm. I stand and listen, and slowly, I begin to match it. My breathing softens. The world around me fades into the flow. The river is not just something I hear– it surrounds me, holds me. It feels like time moving without hurry.

I stand at the riverbank; the sun is setting, casting long yellow shadows through the trees, causing the water to glitter. A single bird is twittering, somewhere very far away. No one else is out at this hour; cars distantly roll by. I am absorbed by the dull, gentle roar of the river.
Splashing, Screams, Windy. The calm breeze follows with the stream of water. The clash of water as it hits the rocks blends with the sounds of children running around the playground.

All that’s left are echoes of voices no longer heard. I wish I’d taken more recordings. The one I have has been played over and over. I can hear his voice in my head as I fall asleep, only he always says the same thing. Where has the rest of his voice gone? Where have I? Sometimes I try to conjure the rumble of his words, the bark of his laugh. I come up empty. I had resigned myself to living as a vessel. But vessels are meant to hold, vessels channel. Everything I was, everything I held has slipped through my fingers like sand. I can hear it, in endless supply, breaking down the rest of my life into granular moments rushing to trickle away. Escaping. Maybe that’s all I have left to hold— time as it slips away.

The cape snaps open and settles around my shoulders, and the clippers click on with a low, steady buzz that I feel in my teeth before I hear it. It hums against the back of my neck, growling a little louder each time it bites through a thicker patch, then softening as it glides up and away. Scissors snip close to my ear, quick and crisp, like tiny beaks pecking at the air. Somewhere behind me, the shop keeps talking, laughter, a game on the TV, the swish of a broom pushing hair across the floor. Then the clippers click off, a brush sweeps my neck with a soft scratch, and the quiet feels fresh and cool, like the air on my newly bare skin.

Halloween is very different now. The rustling as you dig into candy buckets looking for your favorite candy, the soft hum from those fun inflatable decorations as you admire them, or simply the laughter with your friends as you run from door to door, trick-or-treating. The memories that come from sound go hand-in-hand with memories from photos as well. Even though photos are silent, you can hear exactly what they sound like.

Late night, the dorm finally quiet, but never fully asleep. The radiator ticks and knocks like someone tapping from inside the walls, slow and uneven. Down the hall, a door clicks shut, soft but heavy, the sound sliding across the floor and fading. Muffled laughter leaks through a wall, then stops, then starts again, like a radio losing its signal. The buzz of the hallway lights hangs over everything, thin and constant, a sound you only notice once you start listening. Footsteps pass, slippers dragging on the carpet, then gone. And underneath it all, the low hum of the building breathing, holding all of us inside.

Full Title: The Hand Dryer in Sawyer’s Bathroom
Journal Entry: It’s not a sound, it is an event. You put your hands under it and it just R-O-O-O-A-R-S…like a very angry jet engine. Your skin ripples. For those 10 or so seconds, you can’t hear anything, not even your own thoughts. You feel almost guilty thinking you’re disturbing the peace that readers had before you went into the bathroom. Then it cuts off and the silence comes back even quieter than before. You come out. No one is looking at you. Okay, guess it’s a normal sound here.

Title (no article): Handwashing Scene Gets Cut From the Play Almost Every Time and I’m Starting to Get Concerned
Full Title: The Handwashing Scene Gets Cut From the Play Almost Every Time and I’m Starting to Get Concerned
Journal Entry: The bathroom across from my dorm runs like a looping little stage performance that just resets with the same tired confidence over and over again. The door does its slow creak-swing entrance like it’s being lowered into place by invisible stagehands, shoes slip in soft and unbothered, and the stall doors snap shut too loudly. The flush detonates its one big line—loud, dramatic, absolutely convinced it matters more than everything else in the scene. And right after that is where things get weird. Sometimes the sink is there, technically, a quiet prop in the background; water flickers on for a second, a quick hiss, then nothing. But sometimes it doesn’t get called onto stage at all. Sometimes it goes: flush, stall clicks open, bathroom door starts its slow exit creak—no tap ever turning on, no water sound at all, no whirr of the paper towel dispenser, just the sink completely ignored, actors leaving mid-scene.

We understand that different tones and pitches on guitar are achieved through pressing on different frets, which determine the length of the string that gets to oscillate, shorter the length, higher the pitch. But harmonics are special. By gently resting your finger on the string and quickly lifting off as you pick, you create a clear, chiming sound that rings around your ear. This happens through a carefully controlled placement of your finger on the string that mathematically aligns with the wave equation, signaling that beautiful sounds don’t happen by coincidence.

At first I don’t like the feeling of the smooth synthetic cushion pressure on my ears but Rrrrrrr! PO-W-ER On. Battery: fully charged.       Rrr!  Bluetooth, connected. The default setting is noise cancellation. It’s like a small vacuum is pulling at each of my eardrums. Tdbrshh of fingernail on the plastic outside, it finds a button with a tk and — Aware. Birdsong floods my ears. The air whooshes through the holes on the exterior shell of each ear cup. I’m walking, so the brushing comes in fits and starts. Music begins to play; a beat enters from either ear, back and forth, syncopated. It falls in step with my walking, and with the sharp whooshing of the wind, picked up and amplified by hidden microphones.
The dogs barked so loudly the truck started barking too. What a lovely hocket.

Cadenced, cacophonous, harsh, natural, lively, vivid. This sound comes from a pet, which is a horned frog, whose croaking is very rhythmic especially in the late night. It is quite determined, as for attracting mates or intimidating its predators, I guess? I always wonder what is the specific message that it is trying to convey. I kind of feel the wildness of nature while still staying at home, which is filled with a lot of artificial noises, to also embrace this lively and vivid sound as it is produced by a living creature.

Midnight, the campus asleep, the air cold and still. Then the first strike, deep and heavy, rolling over the rooftops in a slow, shimmering wave that hums long after the hit. Again, and again, each toll steady as a heartbeat, the windows buzzing faintly as the sound fills the room and the chest at once. Between the strikes, the silence feels deeper, like the night is holding its breath. Then the last toll fades into a low, trembling ring, and the quiet settles back in until the next hour calls.

“HOW ARE YOU?” “HOWS SCHOOL?” “HOWS BASKETBALL?” These were the questions I got over and over again as I returned home for the reading period. “I’m good”, “school’s good,” “basketball’s good.” These were the answers to the questions I got over and over again .

Everyone has their own unique “voice.” And it’s not just about language, accent, or tone. It’s the personal mix of timbre, rhythm, and the way each of us speaks. Isn’t it fascinating that we can often recognize someone just by hearing them, even with our eyes closed—guessing their identity, age, gender, or even mood? Emotions are especially unmistakable. They come through more directly than the actual words we say. Whether someone sounds heavy or excited, calm or frustrated, it’s almost impossible to hide. People around us all carry their own distinct voices too. And of course, sometimes two people sound surprisingly similar, which is its own kind of mystery.

Title (no article): Humming Washing Machine on a Silent Day
Full Title: The Humming Washing Machine on a Silent Day
Journal Entry: The campus is empty, and the silence feels wide. In my room, I lie down and press my ear to the floor. At first, nothing. Then, slowly, a sound appears, low, distant, turning. The washing machine speaks from below, its rhythm traveling through walls and floors. It hums, spins, repeats. In the quiet, it becomes everything. A small sound, far away, filling a large emptiness.

It lies coiled, tensed, rattling its metallic tail against the soft hiss of your breath. Or clutches a handful of water as it seeps away into drip, drip, drip. Or flowers rapidly into unimaginable colors, creaking and squeaking and screaming at a frequency just out of sight. Then sometimes it goes quiet.
I can hear the sound my stomach is making right now. It’s an intermittent gurgling…. It also kinda sounds like a screech. Maybe it’s a cry for help. Following the rhythm of my heartbeat.

Title (no article): I Had to Buy Emergency Lip Balm at the Bookstore
Full Title: I Had to Buy Emergency Lip Balm at the Bookstore
Journal Entry: The packet tears with a thin, tensile rrriip. A high-pitched crack that starts sharp and then frays into a dry whisper. The sound has a stretched texture, cellophane fibers pulling apart. In the bare room made of silence, it rebounds faintly, turning a small action into something loud and seismic.

When the cup is lifted, the ice shifts with a glassy clink that sounds both delicate and hard. The cubes knock together in tiny collisions, softened by water, producing a cool and expensive kind of brightness. It is a sound tied to refreshment and ritual, almost cinematic in how easily it suggests a hand, a room, a pause.

Having a conversation while periodically snacking on the loudest chip or cracker ever, that which rattles your skull, damn-near chips your teeth, and overwhelms your sonic processing of anything outside the chip’s singular loudness. A crunchy sporadic interruption that, in the radio frequency context, sounds like a distant trucker calling desperately for help.

Title (no article): IDK Even Know What to Call This Sound
Full Title: IDK Even Know What to Call This Sound
Journal Entry: The sound of Kiki Smith’s voice through a microphone in some sort in an auditorium. Echo? Expansion? The sound of her voice was elongated; rounded; stretched and deeper than how her voice sounded to me without the mic to mediate it. It felt fragile; like if vocal cords were gills and the way they rippled were tired.

Title (no article): In the Midst of a Snowstorm I Am Heading Home
Full Title: In the Midst of a Snowstorm I Am Heading Home
Journal Entry: Snow hits my worn-out tires like whiplash. Outside, the wind growls; inside, the radiator hisses. The sound of metal colliding, crickets whispering, surf swooshing all at once encompasses a small moving space. The county route extends afar, its vanishing point blurred by snow. In the midst of a snowstorm she says—you arrive at your destination.

When you turn on the radio, it means the blinds are drawn. There’s a moment when it’s dark, and the button makes a satisfying click. There’s a moment where the click rings out and you’re in the dark before someone’s voice comes crackling to life over the speaker. Mid-sentence. But what I like most the blankness that follows the click. It’s comforting, in a way, not quite crisp or mechanical, not fast enough to be a pop, but almost like an old keyboard. Familiar.

Title (no article): International Phone Call with Time Out of Sync in the Midst of a Lecture
Full Title: An International Phone Call with Time Out of Sync in the Midst of a Lecture
Journal Entry: I sit in a lecture, trying to focus, when my phone begins to ring. The sound feels out of place, cutting into the quiet. I look at the screen– it’s my sibling. For them, on the other side of the ocean, it is already late afternoon. For me, it is still class. The phone keeps ringing, steady, patient. I stare at it, caught between two times, two places. I want to pick up, to answer, but I already know what I will say again–that we are not in the same hour. The ringing stops, but the tension stays, hanging quietly in the room.

Last week, our biology lab took us to Hopkins Memorial Forest. Walking through the woods, the occasional croaks of frogs brought me back to the story I shared in my first class about the horned frog I once kept. If you listen closely, you can also hear crickets and small insects rustling softly. I even heard the sound of branches snapping, which felt a bit unsettling. The forest is like a labyrinth, luring people in with a rhapsody woven from all kinds of living things—inviting them to explore, to learn, and to evolve.

Title (no article): It Will Never Be the Same
Full Title: It Will Never Be the Same
Journal Entry: Is this an imagined sound or an actual sound that I’m hearing right now? It’s like a white noise. Nonstop. That resembles the sound of my refrigerator. Wi—nnng - Wi–nng- Wi—nng- Wi-nnnnnng… Nor unpleasant or pleasant sound; it just follows me as I walk towards my room. Maybe I need some real sleep.

Like plastic melting in far too hot temperatures, the dew from the trees plops and pitter patters onto the fallen leaves. There are footsteps, voices in the distance, but the gentle drips remain unchanged.

The room breathes in fragments: the soft avalanche of popcorn between fingers and teeth; chairs answer every small movement with a restrained groan; a collective intake breaks into scattered gasps, uneven and late, like waves arriving out of sync; a can opens with a tight, pressurized hiss, too bright in the dark, followed by the wet reset of carbonation settling; someone shifts, fabric brushing fabric with a quiet scrape.

Blowing air into a bottle of juice, the bubbling sound continued to echo inside the paper bottle. The liquid sound of sucking up the juice is also “crazy” as the amount of liquid inside the bottle is reducing… The “bop” sound is finally produced by the tap of air pressure inside vs outside of the bottle. Very interesting.

Rubbing, friction, splashing, tranquil, rhythmic, wavy. This sound comes from this summer when I visited my Brother in Austin. This was our first time kayaking down the river so we were able to experience this for the first time. Beginning with a soft shush to quiet the listener. They are then met with the rhythmic swing between friction and splashes. The vest rubs between itself and the phone, while the paddle dips into the water and knocks on the boat. The trickling of water contracts with the deep knocks of the boat, as a motorcycle goes by in the distance.
The kettle burns itself and the bubbling sound is never a signal to end yet. Becoming. Heavy breath, sweat dripping, dancers’ bodies colliding. “We hold hands in midst of uncertainty”

Tapping on the keyboard next to me and the smug, plump silence dries and crinkles in snapping intrusions. (My skin is dry, too, and so frequencies connect. I feel it in my face). Click and drag. Click and drag Tk. Tk. Tk. Tk. Skin slides over sleek metal, like a sheet of paper gliding to the floor. Keratin nails knock on plastic in irregular cracks. I can’t make out the meaning based on what I hear. For a brief moment, knuckle joints are pulled apart. Typing stops, but a different popping enters. An anxious bottom-feeder glides around its tank, exhaling water from its mouth, scattering the pebbles against the glass. Dig and dig.

As I sit down at my computer, the familiar noise begins to fill my eardrums. My fingers press against the keycaps without rhythm, a cacophony of ceramic clacking against metal at varying intensities. It follows me through assignments, hobbies, and late nights talking with friends. Beneath the clatter, the spacebar lands with a low, hollow thock, marking the end of one word and the beginning of another.

Title (no article): Kinna Sonha: Birthdays No Longer Mark the Passage of Time
Full Title: Kinna Sonha: Birthdays No Longer Mark the Passage of Time
Journal Entry: BLAAAA! Blaring horns, a little discordant and brighter than my still-dormant brain is ready for. Then comes a voice: “Uno, dos, tres, cuatro…” Bumbum, ba-dum ba-da ba-dum. Bouncy baselines playfully interrupted by a nineties sort of screech fill my headphones as I stare at the ceiling. Songs have a funny way of transporting us back in time. I haven’t heard this one since I was small. It was a favorite of my dad’s. He would have been 63 today. But today is just a day. Maybe, 15 years ago, we listened to the very same song together. If I close my eyes, am I back in time? It’s the kind of song that makes even the most stagnant of bodies want to dance. My fingers are twitching, tapping along to the rhythm despite themselves. A second ago, they felt too heavy to lift. My head starts to bob. If I close my eyes, I can see him dancing, socked feet shuffling back and forth across a wooden floor. If I close my eyes and listen, do I remember thinking he would live forever?

A messy, stuffy kitchen. Crackling oil in pans, baselines of music from the speaker. Inhabited by dance moves, bad singing, a shared world. Without announcement, the awkward throwing together of stainless-steel bowls. Sounds full and funny, happening abruptly with inconsistent rays. This makes it funny, Fluctuating: short, long, high pitch, lower. Water sloshing, spilling and dripping. Gelatinous sounds hitting the brain, shared smiles. The sound of unexpected joy from brains being struck in the same way. A shared world
Knuckles rap thrice against a thick wooden door. Succinct sounds in rapid succession. They are unavoidably loud, their resonance hiding the hesitation behind my fist. Am I disturbing you?

Koff- Koff- Kofffff, rustle rustle, squeak squeak, shhhk shhhk…the walls span short and thin. Sniffle sniffle, sigh. Koff, koff, koff, now in my own space. The silence of an eye roll, tired eyes. I want to sleep but the sounds of struggle surround me, inside and out. Rustle rustle, shhhk, shkkk, sigh.

The sound starts slow and mellow. It captures the confusing but wistful beginning of a budding relationship. Despite this, there is an underlying sense of somberness and tragedy. It ultimately foreshadows the eventual ending of the relationship. As it continues, it quickly explodes; filled with feelings of passion, love, and discovery. It highlights the peak of the relationship. There is a sense of being on top of the world, a feeling of how nothing can possibly go wrong. The duration of the song highlights the different phases of Mia and Sebastian’s relationship. From hopeful and whimsical, to romantic and passionate, and finally restrained and somber, it represents the journey of the entire relationship.

Title (no article): Laid Against a Pillow, Hearing Sounds of the Body
Full Title: Laid Against a Pillow, Hearing Sounds of the Body
Journal Entry: It is not that natural, but the sound of the ear and hair brushed against the pillow, I’ve heard it for one fourth of my life now; grimey, crumbling like a pastry does, spiky pink noise, and the ten-hertz sound of one-hertz heartbeats blinking between heard and unheard. The rest, the sound of a forest. Hair is leaves rumbling and grass sweeping against the wind. the noise of dormant quiet. I can hear me blink.

At night the bus lowers itself with a hydraulic sigh, opens its doors, and idles in a thick diesel murmur that seems to stain the air. The sound is heavy, tired, and public, carrying the weight of schedule, labor, and return. When it pulls away, the street suddenly feels too open, as if the machine had been holding the dark together.

It's a late night, spent catching up on readings and homework. I was in Paresky until it closed at 1am, then I migrated to the reading room. As I worked myself to exhaustion, the sound of rain tapping the glass windows accompanied me. A near-constant pitter-patter, just loud enough to keep me awake through the night. Sometimes, if I stopped to listen, I could convince myself there was a pattern to it, but it would quickly prove me wrong. The sound accompanied me throughout the night, and before long it was time to head home and get what little sleep I could. The sound followed me home, up the stairwell, and soon I found myself falling asleep to it. If only I had brought an umbrella with me.

Sniffle, dragggg dragggg, plop, slam, sigh. Click click click time is 9:40, sigh. Rustle rustle rustle, click, slam. Pitter pitter patter patter click, pitter patter step slam…skirrrrr swoosh, water runs, click clack, rustle rustle rustle, shut off…pitter patter step step click, slam, rustle rustle. Sniffle koff, sniffle koff. Late to class.
A slight hum grows into a groan. Water floods in, sloshing with uneven sways. The machine shutters, but then begins to churn. Rhythmic pulses emit. Whirring, whirring, whirring.

The washer door thunks shut and the machine fills with a rushing hiss of water, like a faucet running somewhere inside a wall. Then the drum starts to turn, slow and sloshing, clothes slapping against the sides in a lazy, heavy rhythm. Across the room a dryer tumbles on its own beat, a zipper clinking against metal every few turns like someone tapping on a window. When the spin cycle kicks in, everything builds into a deep, rattling roar that shakes the floor under my feet and buzzes up through my shins. Then a sharp buzzer cuts through the noise, the drum slows to a few soft thumps, and the room settles into a warm, humming quiet.

The washing machine begins with a slosh, but the final spin sharpens into a centrifugal whine that feels almost surgical. Wet fabric thumps unevenly against the drum, creating a rhythm that is half machine timing, half accident. The room fills with vibration so completely that the sound is felt in the ribs before it is fully heard.
The chime of an alarm, a signal lying in wait, alerting me of fresh and clean clothes. Escaping from my computer's speakers it is an email received, a crossed out to-do list, a job well done.

The air is filled with the layered calls of birds, each a distinct voice but woven into an unbroken, living fabric. A staccato, sharp chirp cuts through the quiet—unrelenting, rhythmic, a tiny beat of strength. Higher, a softer trill, rolling, and liquid, like water over smooth stones. Wings flutter, a moment’s rustle of movement, quiet, and a burst of song. The world is alive with their songs, a conversation shared on the wind.

You are rushing to class early in the morning or trying to enjoy the last moments of your sleep and… WHHHHHNNNEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE…!! It pauses for a while and comes in again through the window: WHHHHHNNNEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE…and it moves around. What did these leaves even do? Must you blow them at this time of the morning?

It’s dinner rush, the room is filled. If I stay quiet, close my eyes, and crane my neck I can almost make out individual conversations. Agreements and laughing amongst the clanging and clatter of utensils—metal on plastic.

Title (no article): Less than a Drop in the Ocean
Full Title: Less than a Drop in the Ocean
Journal Entry: This sound centers you as you walk or as you stay still. It is talking to you; it is telling you about its life, all of its tales, connections, and experiences. The water has been there long before you. It has helped you; it has hurt you; it could destroy you, but here it doesn’t. The waves crash into the sandbar, powerful and uncontrollable. It comes close enough to speak, but it will not touch you without invitation. The sound is ancient and modern and holds the power to consume your soul–disintegrating you into itself. The sound matters because it has always been there. As you walk or sit or lie or stand, it does not stop. It will be there when you are there and when you leave. It has a temper and emotion. The water is watching you as it has watched the world; your problems are less than a drop in the ocean. WOOSH WAAshhh, CRASH, shhaash, SHWOOoo.

Late evening and the library holds its breath, a hush so thick that every small sound seems to echo. Keyboards tap in scattered bursts across the room, like light rain starting and stopping on a roof. A page turns somewhere behind me with a soft, papery sigh, and a chair creaks as someone leans back to stretch. The heating vents breathe out a low, steady whoosh that I only notice when it shuts off and the silence suddenly gets louder. Then someone’s phone buzzes against a wooden table, a harsh rattle that makes half the room look up, and the quiet slowly folds back over everything.

Full Title: The Library Closes in Fifteen Minutes
Journal Entry: Writing stops sounding like writing and becomes friction. Scratch, scratch, a thinner scrape where ink starts to run ahead of thought. Paper flips with a dry flf of corners. Around me, everything starts to resolve into exit music: chair legs drawn back with a rough drag across carpet, a book shut too quickly with a flat clap, a bag zipper biting shut in short, clipped steps. The clock isn’t heard but felt in the shortening of lines, the way my hand compresses words just to get them down in time, letters tightening into each other like they’re also trying to leave.

9am in the kitchen of Susie Hopkins House. The lights in the kitchen all make a fluorescent buzzing; like gnats. The main light is the quietest - the pantry light is the loudest. I can hear its zzzzzz all the way from the main stairs. The noise disrupts the otherwise silent kitchen, which is large and has many windows and faces a snowy, freezing outdoors.

Unfamiliar bird--chirping. Tweeta-lita-lita-lita-lita-lita. Tweeta-lita-lita-lita-lita-lita. It’s definitely in the room, but it can’t be? Perhaps there’s a window open? Nope. It’s loud enough to indicate proximity, yet no bird can be seen. Tweeta-lita-lita-lita-lita-lita. Tweeta-lita-lita-lita-lita-lita. It sounds like a perfect chirp -- almost too perfect -- and hollow. Perhaps it’s in the air vent? Nope--it’s just the new clock.

Title (no article): Listen Closely to the Noisy Sounds I Hear While Eating
Full Title: Listen Closely to the Noisy Sounds I Hear While Eating
Journal Entry: There were the sounds of many people chewing, mixed with the sharp “clinking” of knives and forks hitting each other. Even more piercing than people’s conversations was the scraping of chairs. It was an extremely unpleasant sound, as if it summoned a deep-seated fear from within. I felt as though I could also hear myself chewing—not through my ears, but through bone conduction. The “crunching” inside my own mouth was very distinct, and the textures of different foods revealed themselves through sound: celery is crisp, tomatoes are sticky, potatoes are soft and pasty, and so on. I never expected that eating is not only a feast of taste, but also a kind of auditory concert.

Again in my little cave, ready to sleep early, and there is a high pitch ringing! The noise travels up to me before soft but bright laughter bubbles up as well. I want to sleep and I will sleep as these sounds continue throughout the night. They are happy as a few join in on trying to sing as bright and squeaky as they can, before their voices fall down a few octaves and bubble with laughter.

The sound of peeling an orange is soft and subtle—like a gentle tear or rip, almost papery but with a hint of squish. There’s a light snap as my fingers break through the skin, followed by a faint crackling as the peel pulls away, fibrous and a little juicy. It’s intimate and quiet, like the fruit is sighing as it’s being undressed.

Title (no article): Long Paresky Queue I Seem Not to Bear
Full Title: The Long Paresky Queue I Seem Not to Bear
Journal Entry: The ‘Resky dining hall is full of sound, layered and moving. Trays hit surfaces, voices overlap, machines beep, food sizzles. It feels like too much at first. But then patterns appear. The same actions repeat, again and again. Serving, moving, eating. The noise becomes rhythm. The chaos becomes something steady.

Title (no article): Lover of Music–Dancing Between Two Songs
Full Title: A Lover of Music–Dancing Between Two Songs
Journal Entry: Two songs play at once, and at first they clash. But I stay with them. One rises slowly, the other already strong. My body listens, shifting between them. When one reaches its peak, I follow it. Then the other calls me, pulling me in a different direction. I move between them, carried by both. The lyrics blur, but the feeling stays. It is like standing between two worlds and letting them both move through me.

An exhausted caregiver, bouncing and counting, whispers the beat of sleep to her restless baby.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, niiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiine, ten.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, niiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiine, ten.
Number by number, beat by beat--breathy, bouncy, and choppy--the baby finally rests to the rhythm of life and keeping time.
Laughter, chirping, footsteps. The cool wind cuts through the many conversations and laughter of Pareksy and Chapin quad.

Title (no article): Madeon Chaos Magic, Unreleased Red Rocks Concert 2025
Full Title: Madeon Chaos Magic, Unreleased Red Rocks Concert 2025
Journal Entry: A boom looms back there on stage. Electric space risers and mystery pads, everything pitched gradually up, opening for heavy guitar, busy fast industrial beat. The artist’s distorted lyrics struggle to stay afloat above the swarm of impacts, basses and WWWW. Grimey, grainy, grindy. Sounds of dark red, dark blue, with an accent of blue-white.
The softest all percussion band—a counterpart of the tiniest violin, viola, cello trio— playing a composition of comfortably soft and low-ended fuffs and dunts.

Silent, meditative, rustles. Clop clop clop down the aisle. The wood receives the body, soundless. Bells, incense. It should feel warm, but it always feels cold. Hymns break the air, murmurs in the pews. The collective whisper of the rise and fall, kneel and rise and fall.

You start by hearing my dad’s voice, “sabrosos tacos de canasta al estilo Guerrero.” He’s projecting, advertising, with a lot of staticky background noise caused by the nearby freeway: wind and cars. My voice enters. Talking to the audience, explaining, “nos callo la ciudad.” Laughter. The words aren’t good, but we laughed. My dad explains, “pero aqui segimos vivos.” While my dad advertises our new location, you can hear the rumbling of a car pass by. You can hear my breathing, laughing but keeping it in. Alternatively, had the recording been earlier, it may have been panicked breathing. You end with my statement, “We’re at a different Home Depot.” Matter of fact. It was inevitable.

A swelling ocean of voices rises and falls in overlapping waves. Forks scrape plates with thin, brittle chirps while trays clap loudly onto plastic tabletops. Grease crackles faintly somewhere behind the serving counter as metal pans clatter and slide. A chaotic chorus of chair legs dragging, soda machines hissing, and bursts of laughter ricochet through the crowded room, constant and restless.

The key jingles as I take it out of my pocket, fumbling the lock a couple times before it slides into the keyhole smoothly and rotates with a soft kerchunk. As the door swings open with a slight squeak, a familiar soundscape fills my ears. Stepper motors whir in thin, rising whines that sharply rise and fall with every change of direction, while the part-cooling fans push out a low steady shhhh beneath them. Over it all, the nozzle skitters across the bed in tiny ticking strokes, and the heated bed rumbles back and forth like a slow train. Over time, the sound has become almost comforting to me.
[lunchtime, right ear to skull] Sponge. Sharp sponge. In between teeth, moist. Squelch squalsh squelch. Squelch squalsh squelch.

Walking past the dormitory eaves, I heard droplets falling to the ground—repeating, uneven, forming their own quiet rhythm. When I looked up, icicles were slowly melting. In the wind, I could almost hear a faint glass‑like cracking, as if winter itself were loosening its grip.
Two heavy circles of metal. Sliding on a ribbed bar. A clean and satisfying sliding…CLANG!! The two 45 plates collide and shatter any existing silence.

Loud, abrasive, metallic whirring. Cordial, jolly banter with some singing of a popular song. Whiny metal cries out in agony with sparks flying.  A low, dull clicking and humming persists throughout the recording. Spontaneous and random. Fun and dangerous. A hard thump as metal sticks itself into wood. Clanging and laughter as the metal misses its target.

Layered. Twang. Booming. Screechy. Wobbly. High-pitched. Meditative. Sustained. Rhythmic. Powerful. A slow, deep beginning with a convoluted horn noise. Adding then a twangy string instrument, like something you might hear from a banjo. Then a shrill, high-pitched, piercing horn that shakes your bones and puts your hair on edge. Adding in a drum theme, almost as if you are listening to the rhythm that soldiers feel and hear as they march to their deaths for their country. Culminating into a cacophony of noise that feels interspersed and individual yet coherent and purposeful. The end result creates emotions of summiting the mountain top, completing a Sisyphean task, while at the same time producing a feeling of immense sadness and loss. The final couple of seconds give a feeling of closure and relief that it’s finally over as the instruments fade to a single horn.
A guttural rrrrrrrrah. Rrrrrrrrrrgggrrrrah. Rrrrrrghrahhh. And a high pitched eeeeeeeeeeeehppppphhhh.

Bow across string, she’s haunting. Familiar, I know this song, I’m swaying across the dance floor in a field of flowers in full bloom. It’s the background to any rom-com slow-motion moment where they finally run to each other in the rain in a crowded room in an airport.

“CH-DING” As I enter the dorm of Greylock quad, out of breath in an understatement. Having walked from the art studio, I was exhausted. I then had to walk up the 4 flights of stairs with my 50 pound backpack. HUFFING AND PUFFING HUFFING PUFFING I finished reaching the top as my feet clapped against the stairs. CICHING. As I took my room key, you can hear the sound of the door unlocking. The mission was complete.

Fishes, water jugs, Game Ready recovery device. What do all of these three items have in common? Their unique versions of the same sound. From the slow, deep and powerful blublub from the water jug to the quick aggressive speed of the game ready. All three are different voices of the same noise.

I begin standing on Earth, looking up, full of wind, car horns, the hums of HVAC systems. My ear travels up, burning in our atmosphere. It survives its fiery, roaring ascent and breaks out into open space, hit with a shock of soundlessness. Even the blood circulating through the ear is silent; the void is total and complete. Flying to the Moon takes three days. When I begin, it is a white dime in the void. As I grow closer, it grows larger, pockmarked and glistening in the light of the sun. Turning back, Earth is a single bead in the sky. I gently descend onto the Moon, still with nothing to hear. I kick up moondust; each granule is sharp and fuzzy. No erosion to whet its edges. The craters and dust here were formed some four billion years ago. The silence is total and complete. Not even the roaring heat of the sun can breach this hush; it is boundless. Moving down on the slope of a large crater, the sky shrinks above me. The movement is gradual; the thud of my movement is the only vibration. The twinkling of dust coats me completely; I have been colored grey, absorbing everything.I settle into the wall of the crater. The rock’s silence is more enduring, more dense, than in the vacuum above. Beneath me is an iron core, which makes only the slightest of groans. The Moon warps and bends as it dances around the Earth, pulling our oceans and guiding our ships. I can hear the slightest fracture of its plates, a giant yawning and rolling with the rising and falling of the day. If I rest here, I too can linger here in perfect silence for four billion years.

Sitting in the Moonlight Diner on a Sunday morning; it’s packed with families, old folks, and locals of all types. The giggling of children is lost underneath the overlapping chatters. The open floorplan prevents the noise from overwhelming. I sip at my coffee - a small slurp - and clink my fork and knife upon my plate. I scrape jam onto a piece of toast, and bite into it with a satisfying crunch.

I imagine an exponentially fading, microtonal ambiance emanating from the clouds as they delicately and sonically move through the air, eventually disappearing completely. Such an ambiance is the sum of a trillion particles and droplets, each with a different tonality.

Boots shuffle on the pavement, icy snow cracks and brittles underneath my feet. Cold crisp breaths are exhaled, while muffled voices and rustling of jackets trail off. A single bird sings and a feeling of warmth engulfs me. It is bright and cuts through the thin air. For a moment, winter seems to drift away and a hint of spring takes its place.

Vibrant, joyous, heartwarming, kind, full, focused, laughter. Fulfillment through togetherness, reliant on the presence of the other, you are my joy, that is the sound-evoked throughout this entire audio. My aunt, my mother’s youngest sister, the woman who became my best friend, with my three-month-old baby cousin, her son, the newest addition to our family. A slight pause for a cough. Both of them seem to pause to cough at the same time. Baby’s laughter opens the audio, and he mimics his mother’s laugh. Baby’s laugh sounds like it takes up his whole respiratory system, it’s a deep and resonant laugh. It fills the whole room with joy, comfort, and safety. I hear another sound in the background of their laughter, possibly a news station. Mother and baby are focused on each other, it’s as if nothing else matters. They laugh together, pause together, love each other.

I hear them through the wall; the bad wifi connection across the country doesn’t make the difference. Shouting, laughing, using kind words, and joking with each other. She’s on speaker. The phone call is staticky and muffled. Jokes are followed by constant “Hello, hello, wait, can you repeat that. The last thing I heard was…” But that doesn’t make a difference in how they both longed to hear each other’s voices. There are sniffles, followed by high-pitched screams of admiration and love for one another.

Ritualistic, like a chorus, but mundane. Time travels. Distinguishable words. Suddenly, today, surreal and bizarre. Low pitch from the beginning. Like tuning something wrong so the chattering becomes scattered, disorganized, elongated. No longer eligible but meditative.

Title (no article): My Brain as It Falls Asleep
Full Title: My Brain as It Falls Asleep
Journal Entry: Screech! My chair rebels against me as I push it back, screaming in protest as I attempt to stand. 4 am in the 24-hour room, and I cannot hear the silence anymore. The keystroke symphony has faded to white noise, and I can hear my eyelids falling. The stickiness of my contacts against my irises makes for a wet sort of blinking noise over the ringing in my ears. Everything is a haze.

She is screaming at me: “you have stretched me too thin!” eeeeee is the sound of something gushing, accumulating. Like a rubber band being stretched into moments before snapping. She is screaming at me so loudly, it seems the entire track and the surrounding mountain range should be shaking by her volume. Yet only I can hear her. Maybe that makes her voice impatient and desperate. She echoes splashes of solitary pool sessions, the crescendo of gears turning in the fan bike whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, my pulsing heartbeat, the flowing of the blood in my veins, my panting breath, inhaling and exhaling. Her loud voice stops me in my tracks in a shock. I want her cries to stop, and so I stop.
A slow, smooth, melodious glissando, wherein each pristine white flower denotes a different resonant pitch on the same synths used in Hiroshi Yoshimura’s Green.

It’s not the sound I hear, it’s the silence, when, for some reason, it stops. There’s a little shudder, and the whole room drops so quiet that I am forced to listen. That’s when I realize that the fridge was ever making any sound. It gives you time to listen to the silence and sparks again: brrrhummmmm… Was it always that loud? The hum is part of the room, but the abrupt silence? That’s a stranger.

I move chronologically through the highlights of NASA’s audio archive. I begin with recordings of the Mercury and Apollo missions - those early first forays into spaceflight. Grainy male voices from audio tapes sound off; early clumsy communications with the public, those fiery sounds of those first rockets, interspersed with sounds so familiar they feel as if they’ve come out of a dream. As if it’s a shock that “Houston, we’ve had a problem,” was a real sentence spoken by a real person; they’re words so ingrained into pop culture, they feel trite. Later, I hear Discover and Challenger take off and land, the grainy (sometimes female) voices of Mission Control count down to lift off or announce a perfect launch. The voices in these tapes are triumphant. Later, I listen to audio recordings from beyond the stars. The sounds of a star translated into twinkling beeps, or the sound of the Perseverance rover scraping rocks off the surface.

Silence. Everyone surrounding the track holds their breath. A sharp crack erupts as the starting gun fires. A massive roar emits from the spectators. Voices collide in an incredibly chaotic manner all layered and tangled within one another. Spikes pound and tear into the track. All I can think is faster, faster, faster. After a couple of seconds, all sounds fade, except my own breath. Then, the line. One more step and final gasp and suddenly, it is all over. There is a second of nothing, but then the explosion of cheers rushes into my consciousness, pulling me back into the moment.

High pitched, rhythmic. Voice is prerecorded & robotic. Squeaking. Rocking. Metal against metal. Reverberating sound. Heavy, coarse. Soft, overlapping voices. Many sounds at once. The squeaking of the rails & the heavy, rhythmic rocking of the train, interrupted by prerecorded announcements that reverberate throughout the underground stations. White noise. This soundscape is a highly nostalgic one - from childhood to the present the subway is an integral part of my experience of the city. It’s how I got to school every morning - how I get home at night. A soundscape of departing and arriving - anonymity. Sitting in a plastic seat looking into a black pane of glass as the world rocks softly. Overlapping chatter in the background. The train slows - squeaking - then comes to a stop. Footsteps pad on the ground, the world opens briefly. There’s another train across the platform squeaking to a stop. The sound of singing reverberates through the open door, lost underneath the departing trains and everpresent hum of everything. A prerecorded voice - choppy - says to “Stand clear of the closing doors, please.”

Cracking knuckles, clacking keyboard, pencil tapping, pen clicking, underlining, side conversations, pages turning, bags zipping. The laughter of side conversations breaks the tense environment of the library, but in the moments between words the sounds of pages turning, bags unzipping, and pencil tapping pierce the air.

Ambiance, breathing, buzzing. Lying in my bed, the sound of the buzzing air purifier fills the silent room, in the intervals that are drowned out by the cadence of my breath or conversations passing by the window.

The stillness of your body resonates through your skull. Any move you make is amplified; you are hearing both nothing and everything at the same time. You hadn’t noticed the squish your eyelids make every time you blink until now. This feeling of realization continues as you explore what other sounds you have been tuning out for far too long.

Noise-cancelling earplugs these days are too noise-cancelling. Turning on Airpod Pros’ noise cancelling feature, it feels like the entire world is muffled. It’s an eerie experience, that you’re not able to hear anything from the outside, and even your own voice gets so filtered out that it’s hard to recognize your own words. It feels like wearing a snorkeling mask under water, where you only hear your muffled breathing with waves occasionally splashing against your ears that remind you of the sound of water.

The following week I hear three knocks on my door and then feet shuffling away. I open the door and find a vacuum sitting outside with a note that reads “A present for the dictator of crumbs.” I dragged the vacuum in my room, ripped up the letter, and consumed it with my prosthetic belly. In that moment something changed inside of me. I truly became the dictator of crumbs. Switching my prosthetic belly on, I rounded up all the crumbs. No corner was safe. I then detached my belly and banished them to the outside, where I’m sure they met their gruesome death to the morning birds.

How do you describe silence? It isn’t nothing. When sitting in silence you can always hear your own thoughts. Everything around you might be a graveyard for sounds but your mind? You can always hear it. Ever overthought, every emotion…you can still hear it in silence. So is the sound of silence merely the sound of our own consciousness?

The month before Christmas. Sure, Thanksgiving dinner is nothing to be forgotten about. The continuous clamor in the kitchen of pots and pans, coupled with aunts and uncles you haven’t seen in months bickering makes for a chaotic but homey feeling. However, it can hardly match with the festivities that come with the holidays. The sleigh bells jingling, presents being opened, laughter, hugs and kisses, culminate in some of the most memorable sounds.

I arrived already acoustically nerfed, my hearing wrapped in a thick, fuzzy reverb like the world had been downgraded to a low-budget underwater documentary, every voice a distant murmur and every footstep a soft thud, and then Nurse Alice ushered me into the chair with the calm authority of someone about to pressure-wash my inner soul. The irrigation began. Warm water sluiced into my ear canal, and instead of clarity, I was treated to the deeply unsettling sensation of tiny aquatic creatures hosting a jacuzzi party inside my skull, bubbles brewing and popping like a carbonated nightmare, my hearing somehow downgrading from “muffled” to “at the bottom of the Mariana Trench. Or the Bermuda Triangle.” It was a symphony of glugs, sloshes, and swirls. When she spoke—offering guidance, reassurance, perhaps even a prophecy—it reached me warped and wobbly as if through liquid cotton. I smiled and nodded like a deeply confused sea creature. By the time she paused, concerned, everything reaching my ears felt like whale song. She told me (I think) to come back tomorrow to try again, which I interpreted through a combination of lip reading and vibes alone. I left the clinic hearing less than when I arrived but somehow experiencing more, like I had briefly hosted an entire ocean inside my ear canals and it forgot to clean up after itself.

a folder, paper arch
the shape built the sound
or cardstock or aluminum or polypropylene
the unstruck drum rumbling
thunder rolls
pink noise disk scrubbing

It is the first proper day of Spring. It’s mid afternoon and I’m standing in the Meadow of Spencer Art Building. I can hear birds chirping; distantly, children are playing. The sun is bright and warm on my skin. Cars roll past on Water Street.

A soft tap of paddle meets ball and an echo through this tiny valley of a parking lot. A gentle back and forth (they’re new to this), it has a knock, a sproing of sorts, an indescribable slap of a hollow ball volleying its way across the court.

Blood. In my veins. It wooshes with a deeper, sinister sort of resonance. It thrums, pulsing like a base drum through the hollows of my skull. Above it, beyond it, I hear myself gasping for air. Gulping oxygen like water and choking on it. The air rasps against my skin. Grating. Wailing sirens resound, blaring like airhorns until everything fades but the sound of the droplets falling from my eyes. SPLAT. It’s a messy sound, splaying into formless shape atop the once pristine pages lying helplessly beneath me. SPLAT— UGLY! If only all water could sound like rain.

The panting at my ankles feels so familiar, yet I see a new face. HeHuh HaHuh ROOF! The sight warms me like a blanket, and his heavy, friendly breaths repeat methodically in my ears. Pant, pant, pant, hot pants.

It sounds like rushing water. And humming? A robot’s humming. Mechanical blends with the natural to create an eerie kind of dissonance, echoing around the empty parking lot. Where does it come from? What am I to it?

It’s late - perhaps 12:30am or so - and I lie in bed, attempting to go to sleep. With my ear pressed against the pillow, I feel vibrations of music downstairs. The thudding bass is low and electric. In the hallway, two people are talking loudly to one another as they wait to use the bathroom. Though their voices are muffled by my door, in my annoyance, it feels as if they’re standing right above me, personally preventing me from falling asleep.

Scribble, Scree Scree, Sraaa, the scribbles of pen on paper. The shifting of pants, shhh, sssssh, ssshhh. The air is heavy with silence and thought. Click Clack Click CLick…Click Clack…the sounds of fast-moving fingers on a calculator fill the air. Only 10 minutes left until it’s over.

Someone’s looking for a pencil. Zop! Clakknk, clatter. Plastic cylinders click against each other in the meshy zippered pocket. Foot drags against carpet, chair thuds out. Still haven’t found it? They must be looking for something specific. Oh — it stopped.
Silence.
Hard at work now.
Feet rustle, a sniffle. Just wait — no one stays quiet for long. Even in the library, silence is many little movements. A hand dryer in the bathroom. The quiet hhhrrrrssshh of some ventilation unit. Coughing down the hallway. Another sniffle, a pencil falls. The chair is pushed out again,
It’s wonderful to be a senior in this place. No longer nervous, eyes glazed over the computer, hearing what’s around me.

The last two steps are supposed to have a different rhythm. I’ve heard so many imitate, “it’s like a bah BAH!” light and fast. “It’s just duh duh duh”. It’s like a “buh BAM!” Powerful and forceful without being heavy. It’s “one two, no, one TWO”. It sounds like, “da da-da.” Whichever it is, it then it goes silent. Every time, no matter the sound of the rhythm. For a beat, maybe two. Rapid succession of movements, of air being pushed aside by power, all breath being exhaled at once, to motionlessness on the ground. Feet that take flight. The rhythm is broken, but it seeks to fly.
Laughter, footsteps, silence. The in-sync clattering of footsteps marking the end or start of a period. The echo of laughter bounces between my window and the building across.

My ear is on its own now, breaking the active topsoil layer softly in a smooth, almost mechanical circular motion like a coring machine, threading itself down in earthen material and time. My ear’s stated goal here is not the center of the Earth—no, no, things would get weird, and pressure would intensify, too intense for it to handle. My ear, instead, wants to hear solid timeeee; the greatest arctic hits: live cultures of centuries and millennia ago. Its impact firstly reverberates the sound of penetrating topsoil, tearing grass and plant root systems, like old creaky furniture, to the nth degree. As the ear descends, I hear squirming and incredibly hurried mass movement. The deeper down I go, the deeper the register of burrowing and wriggling goes, turning into oceanic hums of baleen feeding time. Down, down, down. After an awe-inspiring journey through earth, I hear a slight cracking and shattering, which my ear satisfyingly recognizes as the sound of the top-level permafrost. Still coring, I break this shell layer, entering a surround sound of an almost-flat kombucha, subtly alive. My ear is satisfied.

Title (no article): Pine Trees in Wind, Through a Window
Full Title: Pine Trees in Wind, Through a Window
Journal Entry: A low sigh, sinking from high up. Whhh-uouuu-whhhhuouu-uuuuou. A static crackle, and a long hush. Each needle a whispering fish, swimming against the current.

A plastic grocery bag caught in a fence chatters in quick, papery bursts, then swells into a fuller flap when the wind rises. The sound is cheap, restless, and strangely alive, as if the material wants to imitate wings without ever escaping its manufacture. It turns trash into a temporary instrument played by weather.

The smell of wet dog panting. Hot breath warms up the area around its whitening muzzle. Fingers running through matted hair, pulling, kneading the knots until they come undone. Click clack click and scrapes of sturdy nails on worn cement.
Did you gnaw at your cage so often that now your teeth stick out at odd angles?
Wagging and wooshing around, you turn and expect me to scratch your lower back. Brittle nails scrape against thin hairy skin. Scratch scratch scratch. Pant Pant Pant. Wag Wag Wag. Scratch Wag Pant. Pant Scratch Wag. Wag Pant Scratch.
Step step step. Click Clack.
Did you think I would stay forever with you?
Your leash scrapes against the side of the doorway, the sound of tension. The panting, irregular. Harder, raspier. A high squealing sound comes from within you with an exasperated gasp following.
Did you expect that would stop me?
Whine. Wueaauuhhhh. Wueaaauuuuhhhhh! . . . Scratch scratch scratch. Wag Wag WAG!

The second floor printer warms up like it’s clearing its throat for a speech or starting an engine for some heavy-duty action. Hrrrk…chk chk chk…vvvvvvvVVVVVV… and then one single page pops out, fwip. It simmers for a while and goes back to sleep, and I kinda feel bad that I woke it up just for that.

The 24hr study room in Sawyer is too quiet, which is the reason I don’t really like going there. Every time you step in, the creaking of the wood panels below your feet screams across the room. Those who don’t have their earplugs in would then look up and stare at you for breaking the harmony between keyboard tapping and pencil scratching, as if it was your fault for walking in. The staring continues until you settle down, take out your laptop, and blend in as you also start typing like everyone else. Then, you wait until the next person to walk in and give the same stare.

Before the room is fully light, the radiator wakes in knocks, sighs, and little metallic contractions. Heat arrives as sound first, the pipes ticking as they expand, each pop a tiny announcement of pressure moving through the building. It is domestic and slightly ghostly, like the walls clearing their throat.

Without putting much thought into it, the soft rain falling into the river is soothing.
    Droup Droup Droup droup Droup droup droup Droup droup droup Droup droup Droup dͩrͬoͦuͧpⷬ bͩlͬiͦpͧ ⷬblⷡᶫoͥpⷬ dͩrͬoͦuͧpⷬ bͩlͬiͦbͧ ⷬblͩaͬpͦ ͧdⷬroup
The river continues rushing, pushing the water down its snake body until wherever the tail of its body is. Bringing my attention to the rain, I realize that perhaps it is a bitter reunion. Rain is back with the river, but it plummets into the river's skin with sharp graceful smacks and slaps. Both know, or perhaps don’t realize it yet that one will abandon the other again and again. With each iteration of the cycle they will separate and reunite, but they won’t ever be how they once were. They are constantly changing, and perhaps that is why they’re both mad and glad.

Tapping, drip, plip, plop. Crisp. Rhythmic. A constant tapping, it’s steady and persistent. It’s not a drizzle or a downpour– it’s what you would call the middle ground.
The raindrops are thick enough to dampen your clothes in minutes but soft enough to move without feeling overwhelmed. It’s almost like thousands of tiny drumsticks striking the concrete floor at random but in soothing patterns.

It’s only a slight drizzle, one you hardly hear. There is an occasional raindrop falling into a puddle, or you stepping into a puddle yourself. Your shoes and socks are wet. You can hear the mushy noise beneath your feet. All you want is for it to stop, to make it to dryness. The thought of a warm shower is appealing. Your footsteps become more rapid, as you walk quickly to your house. The rain is picking up; it’s now a downpour. You can hear nothing but the sound of pitter-pattering on the sidewalk and the rooftops. When you finally make it indoors, it’s back to silence.

Mice are so cute; they’re so sweet with their little squeaks. I look at the cage that houses the growing babies who zip to and fro, causing the cage to rattle. Their little nails skid against the cardboard and their long tails tink the cages wall as they turn and run.
