Wind under paper: a quick intake, then release. Flf flf FLF. Pages buckling on the staple. Edges strike edges: light, misfiring claps. The stack chatters, irregular, like a stuttering deck of cards. A thumb drags along the margin, dry rasp, trying to pin it down. The pen enters: nib to page, a fine scratch that lengthens, breaks, resumes. Between gusts, a brief, fragile quiet. The faint hiss of paper settling. Then the next lift, already underneath.

Beeeep…Beeeep…Beeeep…Beeeep…the repetitive sounds of the machine feel natural now. Beeeep…Beeeep…The sounds of students scanning into any dining hall, eco-cafe- it all feels natural, especially at SNAR. The beeeeping drills an odd sensation into you, like you yourself are the machine. You’re directly connected to it; we all are. The students and the machines become one. Not only here but as part of the system in and of itself. Who is the real machine?

I try to hold it in my brain, near the inside of the skull, near the center of my forehead. It’s supposed to be the sound of restraint. It’s an ellipse. Sometimes blue and gray like the pregnant sky. It pulses in waves. Yellow. Pink. Gray. Blue. Churning deep and heavy, miles of lint tumble in the cosmic dryer. A low rumble is stuffing my temples.

Title (no article): Rhythm I Don’t Want with Route 2
Full Title: A Rhythm I Don’t Want with Route 2
Journal Entry: It is Monday noon, and the campus is alive with movement. Students cross Route 2, heading toward Paresky, their voices blending into a busy flow. Then a car comes fast–too fast–and stops close. A voice cuts through everything, sharp and violent, leaving something heavy behind. It happens again another day. Same road, same moment, same break in the air. My mind begins to recognize it, not as an isolated event, but as something repeating. A rhythm forms, but it feels wrong. This is not a rhythm I want to hear, yet it stays, echoing, returning in memory like a sound that refuses to fade.

Birds in the background squeak as if they are terrified whenever the roaring is loud. The volume rises and falls. It approaches and withdraws, moving violently as if to attack. When the screams come, it falls back. It feels seemingly scary for the birds and lonely for me. The roar is like a mixture of rainfall and crumbling of dry leaves, like in the woods when you walk alone.

A muffled pulse of music seeps upward through the floorboards, bass notes thudding softly like a distant heartbeat beneath my chair. Blurred voices rise and fall below, a chorus of loose, jubilant singing that blends together into a warm, indistinct hum. Metal pots clash and rattle in sudden bursts, their sharp clang dulled by the thick layer of wood between us. The entire room seems to tremble faintly with life below, a muted fiesta vibrating quietly through the floor.

Full Title: A Run to Clear My Head.
Journal Entry: Squish, suction, release! Squish, suction, release. This cycle of sound increasing in cadence as my shoe gently pounds upon the asphalt. Critters in a nearby meadow whisper to me: tzrrr tzrrr tzrrr, snip, snip snip, a cacophony of nature’s cries. I run through a tunnel created by trees hugging me from above, the dark tunnel echoes the squish-suction-release loop from my shoes. The dark, quiet, softness echoes so loudly. The sound of my steps becomes lighter, mixing with the vast space of the magnificent tree tunnel, and the weight in my stomach grows lighter too.

Title (no article): Running Upstairs to My Room Before the ’62 Center Pachedu Event Kicks Off
Full Title: Running Upstairs to My Room Before the ’62 Center Pachedu Event Kicks Off
Journal Entry: I swipe my ID, and the door clicks open, a sharp start to movement. Inside, I don’t walk. I run. The stairs rise in front of me, and my feet meet them in rhythm– step after step, fast and even. The sound echoes upward, following me. There is no elevator, only this climb. But it doesn’t feel long. My footsteps become a beat, my breath joins in, and together they carry me. What could be tiring becomes something else--a rhythm I know by heart, a sound that pushes me forward.

Chatter Chatter Chatter…Wachenheim is over there, to the left…I’d recommend going to Spring Street…Beep Beep Beep Walk Walk Walk…The rustle and bustle of campus with the WOW students liven up the environment even just a little. A change of pace. Suddenly, even as a first-year student, you feel smarter, more experienced, and knowledgeable. Directing lost students, giving them recommendations; they even ask for your opinion.

I’m imagining the sound of my toothache. It’s a throbbing sound of lower hum. The extremely high-pitched squeaking sound is layered, pulsating with the same rhythm as the heartbeat.  It’s like my tooth is crying to pull him out. He’s trying to escape.

The kitchen buzzes with warmth as the hot oil begins to sizzle. Sharp pops echo off the walls as each samosa is gently placed in the pan. The air thickens with the savory scent of spiced ground beef and cumin-laced dough, a rich, nostalgic aroma that clings to our clothes and clutches our memories of home. The oil crackles louder now, announcing each golden pocket as it crisps to perfection.
Laughter weaves through the steam. The crunch—oh, the crunch—resounds as teeth meet flaky crust, giving way to tender, spiced filling. It’s more than a bite, it’s a burst of flavor, warmth, and comfort all at once. Around me, the room fills with satisfied sighs, playful groans of “mmm” and “oh my gosh,” each one a small celebration. We pass plates and stories between bites, our voices rising with each shared laugh.
In the thick of midterms and long days of class, the familiar sounds—the bubbling oil, the cheerful chatter, the joyous crunch—wrap around us like a blanket. Cooking together like this turns our tiny dorm kitchen into something more: a haven of home, where tradition meets togetherness. The stress melts away for a moment, replaced by the simple, grounding joy of food made and eaten with love.

The fierce and loud stomps, claps, and chants radiate through Goodrich. I feel the power of every slap across their chest, every stomp through the ground, and every chant said with such firmness, demanding our attention. Step is much more than just claps and stomps, it’s history, freedom, identity, and storytelling. It carries the stories and the hearts of where it originated, slavery.
Every stomp, whether slowly sporadic and rapidly sequential, sends vibrations through the bodies of the audience. Every clap and chant is so beautifully synchronized. Step isn’t necessarily a music performance filled with singing and instruments, but at the same time, it is. Their hands, chests, arms, thighs, and feet are their drums. Their melodic chants are their song. As they progress through their performance, the crowd fills with excitement for what’s to come next. The audience shouts, claps, and stomps alongside them as some of us wish we could be up there with them. The sense of community is unmistakable. As they carry each other across the stage, flipping one another, following each other’s rhythm, smiling and laughing together on stage. Their love and enjoyment resonate from their stage into the audience.

On a slow Saturday, boredom opens my ears. In the bathroom, small actions become sound. The brushing of my teeth repeats, steady, like a quiet drum. Water hits the sink in bursts, and I begin to play with it, on, off, on, off, letting the faucet speak in patterns. The toilet answers with its own voice. I flush once, then again, then again, each one echoing, swelling, fading. It feels like building a rhythm out of water. Then the shower begins, a constant stream, softer but endless. The room fills with sound, and I stand inside it, listening, as if the ordinary has turned into music.

Repetitive striking, but it’s rhythmic. Starts fast, with feet hitting the hard rubber. Pushing with the feet makes the slats turn faster. Hold it. Hold it. Hold it. Breathing that matches footsteps, slats turning, rhythm. Hold your rhythm. One foot in front of the other, striking. Tap tap tap, but it’s more, push push push. Hold it.

Crisp, snip-snip-snip, sharp, quick. The scissors before every cut take a deep breath. The quick yet sharp sound echoed through the room. Quick and precise snips were made as the edges were trimmed. The snip of the blades left a bold statement.

As my fingernail drags along my strands of hair, crackling noises transduce through my skull. The curly terrain my finger travels on is not constant. So, as it dives and jumps from different sections of my hair, there are breaks in the sound, and then louder pops erupt. To a bystander, this action creates little to no sound. But for me, it is a constant symphony of snaps echoing throughout my head.

A distant humming. A buzzing, if you will. A fan? It’s all in the background, dragging itself to the forefront of my mind as I try to concentrate. My eyes are drawn up to face the unforgiving glare that enters my vision like a scream. Every so often, someone coughs or turns a page. A blip, whiting out the sound of the LEDs. A softer sort of sensory input. Tactile. Less laser-like. If you listen closely, you can hear the air blasting through the bathroom hand dryers down the hall. Violent. Still, all I feel is the sound of the fluorescent lights.

My task is to create stretcher bars for a canvas from two strips of wood. To do so, I must first don thick earmuffs - large and unwieldy, they muffle the whole world. With a push of a button, I turn on dust collection - a great clanging begins, largely audible even through the earmuffs. Carefully, I place my plank on the chopsaw, measure my cut twice, and turn on the saw with a squeeze. More violent whirring, banal by this point. It takes mere seconds to make the cut, and I release the saw. It slowly spins to a stop, and I turn off dust collection with another press of the button. Quiet again.

Seal carving is a form of traditional Chinese calligraphy where you’re essentially carving characters on a stone. When carving, different types of soapstones make different sounds. A Qingtian stone, usually green, produced in southern China, makes a crisp, high-pitched sound as the knife digs in and scrapes across the surface. Meanwhile, an Indian stone, usually with an earthy tone, makes a dull, lower-pitched sound as you carve. Good carving should also sound continuous and steady without sudden change in pace. If all of a sudden you hear a quick, sharp squeak as the knife slips over the surface, then you just ruined your carving, and you better start over.

Healthy, rather willful razor. WIDE sound overwhelming. It is subdued, pressed into the skin. The mechanical sound like-a-bee annoys, slightly frightening, but appreciable. Water sounds, crisp and clear, from the tap, with the ease of a running record.

The sound reminds me of home with the farm and all the sheep.  Growing up feeding them in the winter etc… The sound is of multiple sheep baa-ing.  First there is one followed by another.  There is a sense of urgency in the tone. The volume is sharp and loud. It can create a sense of wanting to help or comfort.  The sound is unique and simple.

Shiver shiver shiver, clack clack clack, shiver shiver shiver, clack clack clack. A seemingly endless cycle of forced steps through a cold blanket. A laugh to your left, a snicker to your right; footsteps are with you, all bickering about the cold. Almost there, click clack, click clack, haaaaaa….shiver, shiver, sigh. Finally, we can get out of the cold.

SCREEEEEEECH…The shower curtain screaming as it rakes along the metal bar. The metal hooks clanking together before you pull the curtain. Ironic that something as relaxing as a hot shower is preceded by screams.

The rush of water falling to the hard floor.  The scratching of metal rings brushing against a metal rod.  The clanging of the shower head being moved forward.  The water being broken up by the softer surface of the human body.  A constant noise without much excitement. Soothing when played at a lower volume.

Eeeeeeeeeeeeeeh—a high-pitched screech that never ends. It fades and morphs under the shhh of the shattering water droplets. They pelt the floor, my body. Gather and swirl and disappear. Water turned off, the screech echoes between my ears.

A deep, low rush—a sound anatomically maternal—like fluid rushing omnidirectionally, subsuming my worries through its provision of an oceanic ambiance in the face of restlessness. While I sit at my desk, somehow distracted by ambiance, simultaneously I am in the tank, in the belly of it, but then a squeak, an abrupt stop poses a sonic green light to enter the now humidified intimate space of excretion and cleansing.

Silence is loud. Silence is loud in which it can tell countless stories. The lack of something, in this case sound, somehow can be interpreted in many different ways. Silence is you and a parent after an argument: unable to say anything else but think about what was just exchanged. Silence is shock: being told devastating news, unable to bring yourself to say anything. Silence is happiness: surrounded by people you care about, you take a couple seconds of silence to realize how much you appreciate their company. Silence is confusion: you don’t know what to say, so you simply give up.

A particular kind of silence comes with the snow. The sound of everything else becomes amplified: the slow, controlled breathing to keep yourself warm as the air extends beyond you; the cloth friction as your jacket rubs against itself when you walk, creating a repetitive but rhythmic pattern; the dense crunching of snow beneath heavy boots, or lack thereof with soft, powdery snow. Yet, these sounds go unnoticed, unheard. Despite the bitter silence, it is loud, and you are left alone with that loudness: your own thoughts.

I believe this big room is silent. I try to hear what that sounds like. There is a faint constant exhalation of air from an electrical closet, or distant refrigerator, no, both. A faint click, like the tick of a clock, but peculiarly it does not repeat. Ah hah! Finally, another tick! Ping! Even fainter than the first. There is an even fainting click-clack of keyboard typing, but there are no people or computers in the building? The pale orange light of the fluorescent lamp is humming. Even the bookcases seem to be sending sound waves to me. Am I going crazy? I may have listened too hard. Or paid too little attention the the soundscape until now.

The foreboding sound that sends shivers up and down your spine. Tells you to “get out of the way!” with no words spoken. It never ends until it gets to its destination, but being closer and following it is worse than merely hearing it. You never feel free no matter how loud or quiet, how close or far. The consistency in every moment you hear it, those constant shifts. Forced to see flashes of red and blue no matter if your eyes are open or closed. Even a distant reminder of the sound is enough for you to imagine those red and blue flashes.
Walking through an orchestral overture or a seismic crescendo of a million shattering mirrors and windows.

Purple hush on the descending rings of the horizon. Flowers of silence brushing against the little rustlings of the air. Dim, flighty thoughts like a cloud of gnats, all around, soft. Everything just out of earshot, out of reach.

Water glides steadily over stone, a soft and endless rushing that folds into itself with gentle repetition. Light wind stirs the leaves overhead, drawing out dry, delicate rustles from the branches. Birds call intermittently from the trees, their voices clean and distant in the warm open air. The whole landscape hums quietly with sunlight and movement, slow and untroubled.

A small alarm rings
 sharp and bright,
 like a thin line of light
 cutting through sleep.
A hand reaches.
 Silence falls.
Feet press into snow 
 soft, slow,
 a hush with every step,
 like the earth breathing out.
Sticks snap and crack
 under weight,
 dry bones of winter
 breaking in the cold.
Then water 
 a river rushing,
 full and alive,
 its voice growing clearer,
 rolling over stone.
Far above,
 a helicopter hums 
 a distant, turning sky 
 circling, fading,
 dissolving into air.
Snow again.
 Step.
 Step.
A zipper slides 
 a quick metallic whisper,
 closing warmth around the body.
Heavy boots land hard
 on a hollow log 
 a deep wooden thud,
 solid and echoing.
And back to the snow,
 soft and steady,
 the world quiet again,
 only the rhythm of walking
 and winter listening.

A falling rush of rumbles, running like water over surfaces, splashing back. Ricocheted, flailing, the longing of a mechanic heart. Thumpety-thump- thump-thumping up there somewhere, passing the world by.

Popping, fizzling, crackling, delicate, soft, subtle, ambient, light, electronic. To begin there is a soft crackling and popping of the wood from the fireplace. After a couple seconds light music begins to play. It is a guitar. Very subtle electronic notes also come into play. A voice begins to sing, David Gray. The fireplace continues to fizzle in the background. A feeling of warmth falls over you. The singer’s voice helps to put you at ease and the whole world seems to slow down. His voice is smokey but sweet.

It’s around 10pm outside Spencer Art Building. I am about to go home, done with my work, but linger underneath the building’s awning to smoke a cigarette. It is beginning to snow gently; a fresh, powdery inch has already piled atop the packed ice which has accumulated throughout the winter. The snow muffles everything; my footsteps (I begin to pace) crunch gently, and I can hear the sound of myself breathing. Though I see cars pass by the street, the sound of their wheels cannot reach me. I feel as if I’m in a dream.

Twirling, kicking up, and drifting back down the snowflakes are so gentle as they lay themselves on the ground on top of each other. There’s not many of them, and yet I know soon they will decorate everything I see eventually. From silence, as I walk out into the cold morning it feels as if there’s cheering. Chirps. Bursting and short. Drawn out and repeated by others. To the eye they’re invisible. But to the ears they are everywhere and everything. Despite such an open space they fill it up with COO COO TWEE TWEE CAWKII CAWKIIIIIII EWWOOOOO EEEWOOOO TWEE TWEE TWEEE COO COOOOOO CAWKKIIIIIIII.
Despite how bright the sounds are, there is a sharpness to their quickening TWEEES TWEES EEWOOOO CAWKIIIII’s.

Slice, crunch, silent. Squeak, crunchheeeeee. Breath breaks the silence, then a crrrr-ack, metal on ice, then metal relaxing into the snow. Soft, pillowy, untouched. Broken again, not violent, welcomed, but striking. Finding a path through, forging a path through. Each buried branch is a hidden treasure of a warmth past. In the clearing, nothing hides, all is to see, and everything is hidden. A plain of emptiness, of buried treasures. When will they crackle to life again?

At night, the campus becomes quiet in a different way. My footsteps sound louder, clearer. Each step lands and echoes slightly, as if the ground is listening back. Small sounds appear, wind in the trees, a distant door, a faint hum from somewhere unseen. The silence is not empty. It is full of small voices. I walk through them, noticing everything.

Title (no article): Some Belgian Pop Song, Heard Once, Never to Be Found Again
Full Title: Some Belgian Pop Song, Heard Once, Never to Be Found Again
Journal Entry: Muffle-attacked metallic keys that feels like a dusk taxi in the rain. 80s french disco, with all its rolling toms, young man’s headvoice. an electric keyboard in a totally stereo jungledrum room. Vhs synths reversed underlaid.

The wind is just coming right inside my room like my window does not even exist. I can clearly hear the loud whooshing sound outside. Every three seconds. Whoosh. Whoosh. A few seconds later, I heard my door rattling. The hinge right next to the doorknob rattles as the wind comes through my room intermittently. Posters that I put on the window fall as the air touches them. A slight sound of swishing. I can hear them landing on my carpeted floor, making the slightest ‘tick’ sound. As I hear a loud whoosh and gush from outside again, I anticipate my door to rattle in a few seconds, somewhat rhythmic.

Zz—????—zzk—?—then a thin, teeth-on-teeth hesitation. It moves in snapshots: ziii… zhk… zt, fabric tightening in small, irritated breaths around each failed inch. When it finally gives, it doesn’t glide. It argues, a dragging rattle that keeps breaking, never quite becoming continuous.

It opens with a slow, airy swell of instruments. Soft, sustained tones that feel like a horizon widening. Her voice enters low, smooth, velvety. The melody moves slowly, gliding rather than stepping. The sound is spacious and nocturnal—cool, silver, wandering. It feels like distance: someone’s voice in memory, and the quiet pull of the moon somewhere far above us both.

Title (no article): Song Written Out in Sheet Music for Piano Transcribed from a Familiar Personal Melody, MIDIfied
Full Title: Song Written Out in Sheet Music for Piano Transcribed from a Familiar Personal Melody, MIDIfied
Journal Entry: The melody draws back again and again. Like a pulley. The whole thing in piano but with so much release it sounds like noontide. Taps coming out from weakness. The resolution, always in minor except when the major root note tries to come in with a faux pas, shifts the whole song mellow. The whole sound is narrow. Crescending notes in progression.

When you think of sound, you usually think of music. Music is a lot more than notes, words, and instruments compiled together forming sounds that you like. With those sounds, it carries tone, personality, joy, and memories. There is a reason you’d rather listen to loud, extremely bass-boosted music at a rock concert, and soft, cheerful music at a wedding reception. Music fills the room in a way that no visual can.

The sound of the night envelops like a mist, and now it quickly pulses against us. A wavering hum that stretches far away. Clear and close, two frogs coqui for our attention, their notes doubling against each other. Each drop of sound multiplies, fanning away in concentric circles that sync and throb. Far away, birds call like bells. Like songs. Like tinkling metronomes, above the static of insects.

My afternoons are filled with sounds of joy. Around 3pm, I start to hear them, shrieks like seagulls and melting ice cream. It’s kids at the daycare, they go out for recess and fill my head with wonder.

Harmonious guitars and singing. Rhythmic, high-tempo, vibrational swings go back and forth between deep and high. This sound encourages dance, movement, and sway. It elicits feelings of warmth, joy, memories of family connections, get-togethers on the iconic porch at Kerem Hatemanim (Yemeni quarter), and a yearning for a historical age right before my time- a simpler time. It makes me miss my grandfather.
The sound of 2 guitars begins playing rhythmically and harmoniously. Two voices of men begin singing, warmly, gently, deeply, but also energetically, and in Hebrew. A melody score forms, and is repeated with slight variation each time. In Hebrew the song is titled “A Sparrow Will Call”. At first, it elicits a dry, factual, remembering of past events: family gatherings, proudly showing off my family history, and recently paying tribute to my grandfather. Cold & emotionless state suddenly shatters and my eyes swell up with tears.

Title (no article): Spencer Art Building, 6pm, a Snowy Day
Full Title: Spencer Art Building, 6pm, a Snowy Day
Journal Entry: A soft, high whirr of machines floats above the hallway, a fuzzy churning breath. Voices reverberate around the building, muted, making soft elliptical traveling words whose long tails stretch out in front of and behind them. They reach me round and deep, a deepness that tells me they come from around corners, below floors, and far away.

Recording of snow strippers against Wachenheim utterly outrageous wubb(mm)ing drowning out all semblance of lyrics swings produced by a filter knob rebounded on a massive wall the building opposite the concert when you’re not gasping for air with sharp edges of computerized hi-hats that blurt through.

Thump, pop, thwack, ring, PLOCK! Thump! The ball makes contact with the strings. PLOCK! You feel the ball bending the strings as you swing. A thump or pop is created as the ball makes contact with the wall. A warm rubber ball has made contact with the wall.

The squeal gets louder and higher-pitched before it subsides. It is the sound of regaining lost volume after removing water from the vessel. It is unpredictable and almost seems to have a consciousness of its own as it sucks air back through the perforated top. It makes its presence known with a persistent screech followed by the sound of mini water droplets jumping out of its top and landing on the table it sits on. For now, it appears to have reached a stasis.

I am singing loudly in the staircase. The echo of my vocal cords bounces back and forth between the wall and the stairs, spiraling around me like a harmonious tornado. The percussion of my ascending steps follows the tornado from within me that I am breathing into existence. The lyrics are not in English, and a potential resident entering would get sucked into the storm, but only superficially. The hinges of a door squeak some distance beneath me, I stop the airflow from my lungs, and the tornado twirls and quickly quiets. The remnants are a gentle hum of soundwaves bouncing between my right and left ears.

A stairwell makes every footstep seem more decisive than it is. The heel strike hits first, then the metal rail answers with a faint sympathetic ring, and the whole space carries the sound upward in a concrete bloom. It is an architecture of repetition, where even one body sounds multiplied.

I couldn’t decide if I was pleased or upset when I noticed that waterfalls sound like radio static. It started at a television, or a waterfall. After a while, I pulled on some headphones, but the soft drone crackled at me like white noise, and I changed the channel.

A low mummering rumble drifts over the space. Bright chimes and jingles emit from the registers. Crisp breaks of ice cream cones snap between teeth, followed by a trail of soft laughter. Faint music hums through the air between the rustling of jackets and the crinkling of bags. Customers chatter in the background, their voices weaving in and out of one another.

A deep growl rolls across the sky before splitting open into violent cracks of thunder that shake the walls and windows. Rain lashes the ground in dense sheets, drumming furiously against rooftops and pavement. Wind howls through trees and around corners, carrying loose debris in frantic bursts. Brief silences hover between each strike, tense and electric before the next explosion arrives.

The library holds its sound gently. Pages turn, keyboards tap, chairs move softly. No one speaks loudly, but no one is silent either. All the small sounds come together, forming a quiet rhythm. It feels shared. Even in stillness, there is movement. Even in silence, there is sound.

With every breath my nose crackles and hisses. Every breath feels gross and requires conscious work. Background noise now fades with breath I take, as my own breathing becomes the loudest and most intrusive sound around me.

Good, whoosh, screech, WHOOOOSH, screech screech, whirrrr, slowing, slowing, calm? This is any day, anytime. It is a signal—tell me where we are, how soon we’ll get there. I’m tired, fall asleep? No, don’t be lulled. I’m ready for the day, let’s speed things up. They are already optimized. Things are going smoothly. Are we approaching? Stopping? No, we are on course. We are nearly there. We are on track. We will arrive shortly.

Bright, shimmering splashes crackle against the surface of the pool, each movement scattering light and sound in quick, playful bursts. A faint, sun-warmed haze seems to hum in the air, as distant music drifts lazily across the water, its rhythm softened and stretched by the open space. A gentle trickle from a small fountain persists underneath it all, a delicate, glassy stream that folds into the ambient wash of laughter and movement. Everything feels slow and glowing, the sounds melting together into a warm, fluid blur under the steady weight of the sun.

Bright, easy, sun-baked echoes. Ping. Paddle hit. Yell. Then nothing. Then—pop—plastic on pavement, irregular. A screen door slaps. Laughter—tight and nasal—bursts, then dissolves. A sneaker scuffs. Crushed aluminum skitters across asphalt, spins once, rests. Paddle again. Quiet. Then, a can explodes with a hiss. Not opened. Stepped on.

As I lift my foot from the ground you can hear the connection between the smooth floor and the grip of my shoe separating in a quiet sequence of pops. There is a momentary silence as my foot hovers above the ground preparing for its descent. As my foot travels back down, it is too quick that we only hear the deep thud when it comes to rest.
Vibrations are held in the space, ziiiiiiiii. Chairs and tables slide through the stage among all the harmonious tunes.

BEEEP BEEP. As the nurse took out the temperature stick from under my tongue, it read 101.8. “Goodbye,” said the head athletic trainer, “you can’t practice today.” I got up slowly and methodically, and made my way back to the room. When I finally made it up the stairs, I was filled with relief. HUFFFFFING AND PUFFING. HUFFING AND PUFFING. My body was exhausted as I finally plopped my body against the chair. I feel like shit.

Rubber soles squeak sharply against the painted court, the sound stretching and bouncing off the tall concrete walls. Hollow thwacks of tennis balls striking taut strings crack through the dim air, followed by the softer, fuzzy skitter of the ball dragging briefly across the gritty court surface. A cavernous echo lingers after every hit, folding back into the constant low hum of fluorescent lights overhead. Occasional murmurs and quick breaths between players drift upward, swallowed by the echoing chamber before dissolving into the rhythmic percussion of rallying shots.

Title (no article): Tennis on Clay Through a TV Screen

Journal Entry: Muffled pop, hiss, textured snap. A warmer soundscape during the clay season. The snap of the net as the ball makes contact with it, a player failing to get the first serve in. When the ball hits the clay, it produces a muffled earthy pop. A pop less sharp than on hard courts, it’s more gentle on clay. The shuffle of players’ shoes as they slide across the surface. It’s a grainy hiss that adds texture to the game’s rhythm. VAMOS! COME ON! They shout as they win the point.

Title (no article): Thinking Sound in the Midst of a Cognitive Psychology Midterm
Full Title: Thinking Sound in the Midst of a Cognitive Psychology Midterm
Journal Entry: The room is quiet, but it is not silent. I have finished the multiple choice and now I review. Around me, no one speaks, yet I can almost hear their thoughts. One mind moves back and forth--“A… no, B… maybe A again.” Another erases again and again, the pencil scratching like hesitation made visible. Somewhere, there is a different energy. A quiet confidence, almost loud in its stillness–“I’m getting this.” The room holds all of it at once: doubt, repetition, certainty. No voices, yet full of sound. It feels like listening not with ears, but with awareness.

My ear begins falling through the sporadic windy air as it travels towards the scattered tree canopy. It hears a large gust of wind that wooshes its trajectory into the top of a blooming white sycamore. With its initial velocity it strikes through the taught green leaves with a ricochet of pops before scratching along a sturdy main branch, with its varying layers of bark each sending a tone similar to its depth into my ear. My ear passes by a chattering squirrel that skitters along a neighboring branch as it slowly rolls into another freefalling descent. The canopy is less dense now, and it is coming ever closer to the ground below with an increasingly loud envoy of wind. It all comes to a stop as my ear plops into the wet dirt below without a bounce, but rather a deep squish.

It’s not quite how I remember it. Which makes sense. I am 11,000 kilometres away from all my memories of it. It wraps me up, a dense blanket of grey, soothing me back into sleep. It is gruff and big and gentle. But it is not the thunder from twenty months ago. It is not monsoon in Lahore.

Mechanical watches are a wonder because they transform movements, a kinetic energy, something intangible into something tangible and visible. If you hold it against your ear, you can hear the escapement working tirelessly. It is what makes the ticking sound–a monotone, fast paced “tick tick tick tick…” sound that beats roughly 5 times within a second. The pallet fork, a T-shaped lever, catches and releases an escape wheel that works as a gear, determining how much energy gets released on the second hand. If you also quickly rotate your wrist, you can also hear the rotor, a heavy pendulum, spinning inside the case, making a squeaky sound that goes from fast to slow until it comes to rest again.

Cars anxiously wanting to go forward on a simple road, yet among the rumbling that pushes out more and more smoke there is a bright singular source of sounds. Rings, blings, tink, bink, bink. It repeats. Wheels on structure unfit for it, bumping, jumbling, bouncing the bells. It’s an indication of a sweet treat moving, pushed. Calling out. A BEEEEEEP far away to the ring, bling, tink, bink, bink crossing. How much cash do I have?

The approach is quiet and delicate, barely making a noise until it comes into contact with the smooth, wet roof with a squish. The tongue has now merged with the roof of the mouth through a barrier of saliva, which you cannot hear, but you feel the built-up tension similar to that of a wet suction cup on a glass table. As you begin to release the tongue from its newly joined partner, you hear drips of breaking bonds that build and crescendo in an ultimate clicking release.

Shhhhhhht. Shhhhhhhhhht. Shhhhht. Shhht! Shhhhht. The papers become soggy as they’re placed in the container of water and glue. After working on a costume for so long, I’m playing with paper. Shhhht. ShhhhhhhhtOOOWEEEWOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO
It is loud. It is disorienting. Red and blue flashes as the sirens scream, breathe, scream. As quick as they had appeared they were snuffed out. Yet the lights remained. Some people just drink too much.

Yelling, Cheering. Quit murmurs circulate the track, the suspense of the gun hangs in the air. Then after a few seconds, BANG! The track erupts into cheers. The yelling follows the runners as they huff and puff after each step.

As it grinds along the metal rails, the old wheels call out in pain. Every imperfection in the pathway is felt by them and reverberates throughout the train in a rumble. Moments of silence are present, but do not last long. The only constant is the uncertainty of when the next bump will be.
Droning. Harmonic. Trains warble as they depart in the distance, shaking my window from miles away. Is this the sound of leaving?

Sand. Rehoboth Beach, Delaware. In freefall, my ear picks up the turbulent wind of the air. Whoooosh. The distant reverberations of carnival rides saturate the air in a melodic pattern that contrasts the chaotic rhythm of the wind. On the surface of the sand, millions of grains hit my hits as if beads of rain are falling in succession. Shhhhhhh. As my ear lowers into the surface it glides through the hot layers of sand like rubbing a sleeve together. (Rub Sleeves) This is paired with the thump of footsteps from above thump thump thump these forces echo into the earth. Moving away from the sunlight, my ear pushes through the cold rock, squeezing past like it is a rubbing balloon. Err Errrr Err. The pressure of the weight above grows too heavy, my ear can no longer move…Silence.

Muted, alive, steady. Hours, hours, passing hours, a steady peace. Clicking, pause, clicking, click, click, click. Done. Next thing. Movement in and out, a whoosh of cold air, warmth again. A name called out. Called out again. Where are they? Chomp and stretch, the cheese pulls away, pure delight.

The sounds of a mediocre saxophone performance play over the speakers distantly, sounding more like low buzzing than an actual melody. A baseline to underscore the chatter atop it. Occasionally, the grating, high-pitched, muffled whistle of steaming milk screams its discontent. The volume of the low chatter of these connected rooms seems to rise and fall like waves, with occasional bright laughter punctuating a sentence. Of the speech, nothing is particularly discernible other than the occasional slightly overloud “How are you?!” and “My GOD it’s good to see you.” Everything here is warm.

There is a deep thump in the pipes after you turn the creaking knob. Moments later, water erupts from the spout in little streams that hiss like snakes that have been abruptly awakened. Without your interference, the pressure increases, and the hissing’s volume follows suit as if it has a mind of its own. The water is muffled as it disperses on the bed of the sink, and it takes on a new, quieter form as it softly dances down the drain.

The twilight of sleep, stillness of the morning. Without opening eyes, piercing beeps fill the air from outside. It’s not quite loud, though, or jarring. Just outside, removed enough to not startle, but close enough to pull you from sleep. Rumble of trucks, stillness, then beep. beep. beep. beep. Same rhythm every time, same tone. Beep. Beep. Beep.

Title (no article): Two Friends on a Deadline Typing - a Comparative Literature Class Rush
Full Title: Two Friends on a Deadline Typing - a Comparative Literature Class Rush
Journal Entry: They sit across from me, both inside their own race against time. Two hours and forty-five minutes left. Their fingers move quickly over their laptops, one already at seven pages, chasing three more, the other still holding onto page five. No one speaks, but the room is loud with effort. The typing is not random– it has force, urgency. I can hear the stress in the speed, in the sharpness of each key pressed. At some point, their rhythms meet. For a moment, they type together, almost in sync, like a shared pulse. Then it breaks. One slows, the other speeds up. The sound pulls my mind elsewhere– to an old printing press in a black-and-white film, metal striking paper again and again. Then to a soldier writing a letter late at night, each word heavy with feeling. I cannot remember the film, but the sound stays. It carries memory without needing a name.

Only when it is truly silent and you are alone can you hear the ticks of two clocks marching together. Sometimes you can catch them stepping on each other's toes. Two clocks, far away on either side of the room whose march echoes for me. It’s hard to tell if they are striving to be together or to be ahead of each other.

My task is to fill a silicone mould with wet plaster. In the small plaster room of Spencer’s sculpture studio, it’s quiet. I fill up a large bucket with hot, almost scalding water, then reach into a bin and scoop up a large spoonful of plaster dust, dumping it into the water with a clump. I repeat this process several times until I’m satisfied with the consistency - that of heavy cream. Then, I place a funnel in the opening of my silicone mould and pour the bucket inside. Gloop gloop gloop gloop.
Irregular, bouncy taps. Hollow. Rapid, and then slow. Occasionally, a gentle clinking. Over and over and over and over. Is this music?
A breathy exhale, continuous. Its center is hollow, compact, its edges leaking echoes from within. A thick, metallic hiss. The longer you listen, the more it seems to sing.

I hear my mind collect itself and return to a version of reality, “I must vacuum.” It has been too long since my floors were purified. My door swings open with a rusty squeeze like a dry breath begging for water. I shuffle along the carpet floor in search of the communal dormitory vacuum. The vending machine hums with a flat electrical patience, then suddenly breaks into a clunk and spiral rattle when a bottle drops. Its constant drone disappears into the hallway until the mechanical action interrupts it, making the machine audible as labor instead of furniture. It sounds like industrial convenience industrialized, cold air and plastic waiting behind glass.

I attended my friend’s viola recital. The half-hour of classical music lifts me into another dimension. The music hall is completely silent save for his singing notes, low and mournful. His long fingers dance at the neck of the viola, as his body sways and jerks in time with his notes. It sounds like a lament, and brings my mind to scenes of tragedy.

Disney is a wonderland, a place where magic makes us feel young again. The moment I stepped through the gates, a familiar voice reached my ears: “I can show you the world, shining, shimmering, splendid.”  The screams from the roller coasters, the children’s bell‑like laughter, and the crackling sound of fireworks bursting in the sky all pierced through the air around me. In this lively chaos, people finally dare to embrace themselves, to listen to the quiet voice inside their hearts, and to feel joy without worries.

Background almost rhythmic click — “tk”, hushed and soft voice, variance in cadence, variance in tone, half-cut “hi”, pause, filler “uh”, ambience, telephone filter, shuffling, rushed near the end. Hushed, downlooking, somberly-twinged female voice—a voice associated personally with sleepy, bilingual before-bedtime songs—clarifies that she is, indeed, your mom and, indeed, still can be reached at the same phone number, and is, indeed, still living in the same place. Pauses and hesitations are filled with “uh” on her side, but guilt on your side of the line for not calling enough.

Booming, Crunchy, Bumpy, Enclosed, Metallic. Car door opens, key slides into ignition as a beeping begins, zip of the seat belt and clack of the buckle locking, car door shuts, key is turned and car chugs up, the theme song from “Speed Racer” plays as the car starts. Click of the headlight knob. Thump of the shifter. Car accelerates. Beep as the check-engine light come on. Accelerate, blinker and turn, accelerate, blinker and turn, accelerate again, song ends and door shuts. Am I Speed Racer?

A crow barks in the distance, unseen. Two cars pass by, tire on asphalt, a grinding that sounds like how a mucus-filled cough feels. The crow still caws, I think I’ve passed it now. A rhythmic thud, step, step, step…occasionally overtaken by the satisfying crunch of red and orange and brown leaves littered along the sidewalk.

Title (no article): Walking along the Streets at Night
Full Title: Walking along the Streets at Night
Journal Entry: My vision is blurred by the neon lights, yet my hearing grows sharper. The occasional passing car sounds like a meteor streaking across the sky—there for a moment, then gone. The rustling of trees and grass in the breeze feels like a lullaby. But on the quietest streets, where not a single person appears, I hear only the sound of my own footsteps—tap, tap—whether on asphalt or on old stone paths. It becomes a moment of being alone with myself. In my mind, I replay the pleasant and the jarring sounds of the past. Imagined sounds blend with the real ones, making the night feel even darker.

You can always hear different rhythms coming from the friction between the ground and everyone’s shoes during team warmup. Starting with A-skip, it opens with a short, light, tap against the ground to lift yourself up and followed quickly by a stronger, harsher screech as your foot lands. Then to high knees, it's a series of quick tap-tap-taps in an ordered manner. Then you get to build-ups. That's when you hear different amounts of toe drags against the ground from different people as they accelerate. Some with just one quick “psss” sound as their shoe drag against the track, some with “pss-pss”, and some even with “pss-pss-pss,” which might be just too much dragging.

A quick ticking every second. Enough times to make anyone go crazy. Yet in consistency there is comfort. While many things aren’t certain, the ticking of a watch continues. Late at night with no other sounds, the quiet tick keeps.

After rain, the parking lot makes a soft tearing sound under tires, a long wet hiss that clings to the ground instead of bouncing off it. The sound feels low and wide, more like pressure being smeared than a clean motion. Water changes the friction of rubber on pavement, turning each passing car into a brief brushstroke.

I believe this song is bringing people together, especially around the Thanksgiving/Christmas season. During the Christmas season, this song is heard and recognized by people world-wide. This song is filled with electricity, as the sound vibrates, and attracts the listener. There’s a smooth melody and pitch that makes the listener sing along as well.

Walking back to my dorm room. Lorde’s new single “What Was That” is flowing through my earphones, which I only plugged into my left ear.  I say, “This is the best cigarette of my life.” I can hear the tree rustling and wooshing from my right ear. Sound of sadness. Sound of loss. Sound of longing. A sound of feeling completely empty and drained.

A high-pitched “ring-ing-ing” sound burst out from the opened door. I immediately shut the door. The horrible sound then disappeared. So scary! There’s no sign on the door indicating it is only for emergent use but the sound should be correlated with my act of opening the door. How embarrassing. I could still hear my heart beating heavily in the thought that I might have caused a disaster. Luckily the sound disappeared after I closed the door, which is also quite weird meaning this isn’t the fire alarm. I am still wondering what sound it is.

Jackie’s being too loud in the kitchen making noodles; I can hear the pots clanking. The annoying metallic sound don’t stop for a while. Jackie finishes cooking their noodles. The new sound begins right next to me. Jackie starts slurping noodles, using a metal fork to eat directly from the metal pot—Clink, slurp, glug, clink, slurp, glug, clink, repeat. The final clank sound ends with Jackie dropping the fork into the pot after finishing their noodles.

Title (no article): When You Walk Into the Woods

Journal Entry: When you walk into the woods, the sound of leaves and twigs crackling instantly gets your attention. The further you walk, the more you can hear the stream rushing down the mini waterfall. WOOSH. WASHH. The sound brings you back to life.

Shhhhh chhhhhh shhhh chhhh then quiet then shhhh chhhh shhhh. You feel the cool sensation move through your clothes, through your skin, through every vein and vessel, straight to your core. The wind whispers, but instead of just going through your ear canal, it reaches the innermost part of you. At the same time, it encompasses you. Shhhhhhh chhhhh, feel that chill? It comes and goes and comes and goes…just whispering to you, telling you shhhhhh chhhh through the leaves.

Driving around, listening to some music, I roll the window down and the wind begins to beat. It’s wubbing at a constant rhythm past my ears. The music falls into the wub, it’s like someone’s quickly turning the volume on and off. I’m getting a little cold so I roll up the window, but not completely. This new hi-hat sound enters the mix, so I roll up the window to hear it, but it goes away.

Clacking heels, whooshing air, clicking keyboard. As I sit in a study room, the sounds of footsteps echo the halls. The only constant noise is the whooshing air coming from the air conditioning unit. The piercing sound of the keyboard fills the emptiness.

The first thing you hear is rustling. Leaves? Waves? Surely, small particles aggregated into larger and larger clusters are crashing—gently and perpetually—into each other, massive forces like wind or gravity pushing them together in unintentional embraces. Over and over again. Like a heartbeat. Over top of this endless rhythm, birds coo at different intervals. You are nestled in the middle. Are you the heart of the forest here? The birds are insistent. Abruptly cooing their content. The one in front of you perhaps does not coo, but warbles. Not a shrill, sharp, or unsteady warble, but a vibrational, round, softened projection. Soothing. A heart attempting to escape a chest. A bird’s laugh?

The printer clears its throat and starts spitting pages, each sheet arriving warm, a little breathless, stacking into a soft, uneven shuffle. Then the rhythm sharpens: clean slices snapping down, thin margins slipping away like shed skin. A slower, more careful incision follows at the center, a drawn-out, almost-secret sound as the page gives just enough. Folding softens everything again: a pressed hush, fibers settling into a new shape By the end, it’s all smaller, neater, held. The noise has been folded.
